Chapter 9: Chart Dependencies & Subcharts

Real applications rarely live in isolation. anihpj needs PostgreSQL for data and Redis for caching. Instead of bundling everything into one massive chart, Helm lets you declare dependencies — other charts your application needs. This chapter covers the complete dependency system.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🔗 Dependencies 🎯 20% Exam Weight

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Declare dependencies in Chart.yaml for PostgreSQL, Redis, and more
  • ✅ Manage dependencies with helm dependency update and helm dependency build
  • ✅ Compare Subcharts vs Umbrella Charts patterns
  • ✅ Share configuration across subcharts with Global Values
  • ✅ Import values from child charts into parent templates
  • ✅ Control dependency versions with SemVer constraints
🎓 Certification Domains
Advanced Features 20%

9.1 Chart.yaml Dependencies — Adding PostgreSQL, Redis, Nginx

Chart.yaml with Dependencies
apiVersion: v2
name: anihpj
version: 0.1.0
appVersion: "2.1.0"
dependencies:
  - name: postgresql
    version: "12.x.x"                              # SemVer range
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
    condition: postgresql.enabled                   # Ctrl via values
    tags:
      - database
  - name: redis
    version: "~18.0.0"                             # ~ = patch-level flexibility
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
    condition: redis.enabled
    tags:
      - cache
  - name: ingress-nginx
    version: "^4.0.0"                              # ^ = compatible releases
    repository: https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx
    condition: ingress-nginx.enabled

9.2 helm dependency update/build — Managing Dependencies

Dependency Commands
# Download dependencies (update Chart.lock + download to charts/)
helm dependency update ./anihpj-chart

# Build from existing Chart.lock (no network — faster)
helm dependency build ./anihpj-chart

# List current dependencies
helm dependency list ./anihpj-chart

# Update specific dependency
helm dependency update ./anihpj-chart
⚠️ Always Commit Chart.lock

Chart.lock pins exact dependency versions. Without it, CI/CD builds may download different versions. helm dependency build reads from the lock file — use it in CI for reproducible builds.

9.3 Subcharts vs Umbrella Charts — Pattern Comparison

📦 Subcharts (Recommended)
  • Each dependency is a separate chart
  • Parent chart declares deps in Chart.yaml
  • Clean separation of concerns
  • Dependencies can be updated independently
  • Standard for most Helm charts
☂️ Umbrella Charts
  • One chart that wraps multiple sub-apps
  • All templates in one chart
  • Simpler for small projects
  • Harder to version components separately
  • Consider if you have 2-3 tightly coupled services

9.4 Global Values — Sharing Config Across Subcharts

Use the global: key in values.yaml to share configuration with all subcharts. Every subchart can access .Values.global.

Global Values Example
# Parent values.yaml
global:
  imageRegistry: myregistry.com
  storageClass: fast-ssd
  postgresql:
    auth:
      postgresPassword: shared-secret

# Subcharts access these via:
# {{ .Values.global.imageRegistry }}
# {{ .Values.global.postgresql.auth.postgresPassword }}

9.5 Importing Values from Child Charts

Use the import-values directive in Chart.yaml to bring values from a child chart into the parent's .Values scope.

import-values Example
dependencies:
  - name: postgresql
    version: "12.x.x"
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
    import-values:
      - child: service.ports.postgresql   # From subchart
        parent: dbPort                    # Accessible as .Values.dbPort
      - child: auth
        parent: dbAuth                    # Entire auth section imported

9.6 Dependency Version Constraints

ConstraintMeaningMatches
"12.5.0"Exact versionOnly 12.5.0
"~12.5.0"Patch-level (~)12.5.0 ≤ x < 12.6.0
"^12.5.0"Compatible (^)12.5.0 ≤ x < 13.0.0
"12.x.x"WildcardAny 12.x.x
">=12.0.0 <13.0.0"Range12.0.0 to 12.x.x
📋Chart.yaml depsDeclare dependencies
⬇️helm dep updateDownload & lock
🌐global valuesShare across subcharts
📥import-valuesPull from child charts
🔒Chart.lockReproducible builds
🏷️SemVerVersion constraints

🛠️ Dependency Troubleshooting & Best Practices

🔧
"dependency not found"

Run helm dependency update to download missing charts. Check the repository URL is correct and accessible. Verify the chart name matches exactly.

🔧
Version conflict

Your SemVer constraint is too loose or too tight. Use helm dependency list to see resolved versions. Pin exact versions in Chart.lock for reproducible builds.

🔧
Conditional dependency not disabling

Check the condition: key in Chart.yaml matches a value in your values.yaml. The value must be exactly false (not "false" as a string).

🔧
Using tags for bulk control

Use tags: in dependencies + tags.database: false in values.yaml to disable all database-tagged dependencies at once. More flexible than individual conditions.

9.7 Dependency Conditions & Tags - Selective Subchart Enablement

Not every environment needs every dependency. Use condition and tags in Chart.yaml to selectively enable/disable subcharts.

Using Conditions
# Chart.yaml
dependencies:
  - name: postgresql
    version: "12.x.x"
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
    condition: postgresql.enabled
  - name: redis
    version: "18.x.x"
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
    condition: redis.enabled

# values.yaml
postgresql:
  enabled: true
redis:
  enabled: false  # Skip redis in this env
Using Tags
# Chart.yaml
dependencies:
  - name: postgresql
    version: "12.x.x"
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
    tags:
      - database
  - name: redis
    version: "18.x.x"
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
    tags:
      - cache

# values.yaml
tags:
  database: true   # Enable all DB deps
  cache: false     # Disable all cache deps
Condition vs Tag Logic

For a subchart to be enabled: ALL its tags must be true AND its condition (if any) must be true. If both condition and tags are set, the condition is checked first — if the condition path is defined and evaluates to false, the chart is disabled regardless of tags.

9.8 Global Values - Sharing Config Across Subcharts

The global key in values.yaml is special — it's automatically available to ALL subcharts without explicit import. This is the standard way to share configuration like image registry, pull secrets, or common labels.

# Parent chart values.yaml
global:
  imageRegistry: myregistry.io
  imagePullSecrets:
    - name: regcred
  commonLabels:
    environment: production
    team: backend

postgresql:
  enabled: true
  # This subchart automatically has access to .Values.global.imageRegistry
  # without any import statement!

# In subchart template:
image: {{ .Values.global.imageRegistry }}/postgresql:{{ .Values.image.tag }}
GOTCHA
Global Gotcha: Subcharts can override global values in their own values.yaml, but the parent chart's global values take precedence. Also, global is NOT automatically available to the parent's own templates — you still need to reference it explicitly as .Values.global.xxx.

9.9 Importing Child Values - exports vs imports

Sometimes a parent chart needs to use a value exposed by a subchart (like a dynamically-generated password or service name). Use the exports key in the child chart and the import-values key in the parent.

Child-to-Parent Value Flow
CHILD CHART (postgresql):            PARENT CHART (anihpj):
+---------------------------+        +-----------------------------+
| values.yaml:              |        | Chart.yaml:                 |
|   auth:                   |        | dependencies:               |
|     password: changeme    |        |   - name: postgresql        |
|                           |        |     import-values:          |
| CHILD exports password    |        |       - child: auth.password|
| to parent via import      |───────>|         parent: db.password |
+---------------------------+        |                             |
                                     | templates/deployment.yaml:  |
                                     |   env:                      |
                                     |     - name: DB_PASSWORD     |
                                     |       value: {{ .Values.db. |
                                     |         password }}         |
                                     +-----------------------------+
EXAM
Exam Scenario: "You have a WordPress chart that depends on MariaDB. How do you pass the MariaDB-generated password to the WordPress deployment?" Answer: Use import-values in Chart.yaml to map the child's exported value to a parent value, then reference it in the WordPress template.

9.10 Dependency Version Constraints - SemVer in Practice

Helm uses SemVer 2 for dependency version constraints. Understanding version ranges is critical for reproducible deployments.

ConstraintMeaningMatches
12.0.0Exact versionOnly 12.0.0
>=12.0.0 <13.0.0Version range12.0.0 through 12.x.x
~12.0.0Patch-level flex (~>)>=12.0.0, <12.1.0
^12.0.0Minor-level flex (^)>=12.0.0, <13.0.0
12.x.xWildcard (x = any)Any 12.x.x
>=12.0.0 || 18.x.xOR condition12+ OR any 18.x
*Any versionAll versions (use sparingly!)
Version Constraint Warning

Always use explicit version ranges or pin to specific versions. Using * or overly broad ranges can pull in breaking changes. helm dependency update respects Chart.lock — if Chart.lock exists, it downloads exactly those versions for reproducibility.

10.10 Hooks Deep Dive - How Helm Manages Hook Resources Differently

Hooks are not just "resources that run at a specific time." They are managed by Helm through a completely different lifecycle than normal resources. Understanding this difference prevents confusion when hooks don't behave as expected.

Normal Resource vs Hook Resource Lifecycle
NORMAL RESOURCE LIFECYCLE:
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
helm install → resource CREATED → helm tracks it → helm upgrade updates it
helm uninstall → resource DELETED

HOOK RESOURCE LIFECYCLE:
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
helm install → hook CREATED → hook RUNS → hook DELETED (per policy)
helm upgrade → hook RE-CREATED (even if unchanged!) → hook RUNS → hook DELETED
helm uninstall → hook NOT deleted (unless it's a pre/post-delete hook)

KEY DIFFERENCES:
1. Hooks are NEVER part of the release manifest.
   helm get manifest does NOT include hook resources.

2. Hooks are NOT updated during helm upgrade.
   They are DELETED and RE-CREATED on every operation.

3. Hook failures BLOCK the entire operation.
   If a pre-install hook fails, NO resources are installed.
   If a post-upgrade hook fails, the upgrade is marked FAILED.
   (--atomic will auto-rollback on hook failure)

4. Hook resources are labeled:
   helm.sh/hook: 
   helm.sh/hook-weight: 
   helm.sh/hook-delete-policy:

10.11 Real-World Hook Patterns for anihpj

🗄️
Database Migration (pre-upgrade)

Run Django migrations before new code rolls out. If migration fails, the upgrade is blocked and old version stays running.

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-db-migrate
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "-5"
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: migrate
        image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
        command: ["python", "manage.py", "migrate", "--noinput"]
💾
Backup Before Upgrade (pre-upgrade)

Dump the database before any schema changes. Runs with weight -10 (before migration).

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-db-backup
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "-10"
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: backup
        image: postgres:15
        command: ["pg_dump", "-h", "{{ .Release.Name }}-postgresql",
                  "-U", "anihpj", "-f", "/backup/pre-upgrade.sql"]
Q1
Where do you declare chart dependencies?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

In Chart.yaml under the dependencies: key. Each dependency specifies name, version (SemVer constraint), and repository.

Explanation

Dependencies are resolved by helm dependency update, which downloads the chart .tgz files into the charts/ directory and records exact versions in Chart.lock.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Minimal valid Chart.yaml:
apiVersion: v2
name: mychart
version: 0.1.0
type: application

# Full Chart.yaml reference:
apiVersion: v2
name: anihpj
version: 0.2.0
appVersion: "2.1.0"
description: A Helm chart for the anihpj job board application
type: application
kubeVersion: ">=1.25.0-0"
maintainers:
  - name: DevOps Team
    email: devops@example.com
icon: https://example.com/anihpj-icon.svg
keywords:
  - django
  - job-board
  - python
Q11
What's the difference between helm dependency update and helm dependency build?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

helm dependency update fetches from REMOTE repositories (network required). helm dependency build reads from Chart.lock and the local charts/ directory (no network). Use update to resolve versions; use build in CI for reproducible builds.

Explanation

update downloads new .tgz files and updates Chart.lock. build only works if Chart.lock exists — it uses the locked versions without network access. In CI/CD, commit Chart.lock and use build for deterministic, offline-safe dependency resolution.

Q12
How do you add a dependency from a local file path (not a remote repo)?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Use repository: file://../path/to/chart in Chart.yaml. The path is relative to the chart directory. This is useful for development, monorepos, and testing before publishing.

dependencies:
  - name: my-common-chart
    version: 0.1.0
    repository: file://../common-chart
Explanation

File-based dependencies are resolved from the local filesystem. The chart is COPIED into charts/ during helm dependency update. This is great for monorepos where charts live side by side. The version must match the Chart.yaml of the local chart.

Q13
Your umbrella chart has 3 subcharts. How do you pass the same namespace to all of them?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Subcharts inherit the release namespace automatically. No explicit configuration needed. All resources from the umbrella chart and its subcharts are deployed to the namespace specified with -n or --namespace.

Explanation

When you run helm install myapp ./umbrella -n prod, ALL subcharts are deployed to the prod namespace. Subcharts do NOT get their own namespaces. If you need different namespaces, deploy each chart as an independent release.

Q14
What is the purpose of Chart.lock and should you commit it to Git?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Chart.lock pins EXACT dependency versions and SHA256 digests. YES, commit it to Git. It ensures reproducible builds — everyone (and CI/CD) gets the exact same dependency versions.

Explanation

Without Chart.lock, helm dependency update might resolve different versions over time (e.g., if a new patch of postgresql is released). Chart.lock locks the exact version and digest for cryptographic integrity. Do NOT commit charts/*.tgz files — add them to .gitignore.

Q15
How do you completely disable a subchart conditionally?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Use a condition in Chart.yaml mapped to a values key. When that value is false, the subchart is skipped entirely.

# Chart.yaml:
dependencies:
  - name: redis
    condition: redis.enabled

# values.yaml:
redis:
  enabled: false  # Redis NOT deployed

# Or override at install:
helm install app ./chart --set redis.enabled=true
Explanation

Conditions provide runtime toggling of dependencies. Combined with tags, you can group dependencies: tags: [database] and tags: database: false disables all DB-related subcharts at once. Both condition AND all tags must be true for the subchart to be enabled.

Q2
What's the difference between helm dependency update and helm dependency build?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

update re-resolves versions and regenerates Chart.lock. build uses existing Chart.lock without network access — faster for CI/CD.

Explanation

Dependencies in Chart.yaml are resolved by helm dependency update, which downloads charts to charts/ and creates Chart.lock. Always commit Chart.lock for reproducible builds.

Q3
How do you share configuration with all subcharts?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Use the global: key in the parent's values.yaml. All subcharts access it via {{ .Values.global.xxx }}.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Minimal valid Chart.yaml:
apiVersion: v2
name: mychart
version: 0.1.0
type: application

# Full Chart.yaml reference:
apiVersion: v2
name: anihpj
version: 0.2.0
appVersion: "2.1.0"
description: A Helm chart for the anihpj job board application
type: application
kubeVersion: ">=1.25.0-0"
maintainers:
  - name: DevOps Team
    email: devops@example.com
icon: https://example.com/anihpj-icon.svg
keywords:
  - django
  - job-board
  - python
Q4
What version constraint allows any 12.x.x release?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

"12.x.x" — the wildcard constraint. "~12.5.0" allows patches (12.5.0-12.5.x). "^12.5.0" allows compatible releases (12.5.0-12.x.x).

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Release storage (per revision):
kubectl get secrets -l owner=helm -n NAMESPACE
# sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v1
# sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v2
# sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v3

# Each Secret contains:
# - Chart metadata (name, version)
# - Computed values (all overrides merged)
# - Rendered manifests (the actual YAML applied)
# - Release info (status, timestamps)

# Inspect a revision:
kubectl get secret sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v2 -n prod -o jsonpath='{.data.release}' | base64 -d | gzip -d | python -m json.tool
Q5
How do you conditionally enable/disable a dependency?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Use condition: postgresql.enabled in the dependency declaration. Set postgresql.enabled: false in values.yaml to skip that dependency.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# values.yaml with documented defaults:
replicaCount: 3
image:
  repository: anihpj        # Docker image repository
  tag: v2.0.0                # Image tag (pin in production!)
  pullPolicy: IfNotPresent   # Image pull policy

service:
  type: ClusterIP            # ClusterIP | NodePort | LoadBalancer
  port: 80                   # Service port

ingress:
  enabled: true              # Enable/disable Ingress resource
  className: nginx           # Ingress class name
  host: anihpj.example.com   # Ingress hostname
  tls: true                  # Enable TLS

# Access in templates: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
# Override: --set replicaCount=5
Q6
Where are dependency charts stored after download?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

In the charts/ directory as .tgz archives. Chart.lock records their exact versions and digests.

Explanation

Helm uses if for conditionals: {{ if .Values.ingress.enabled }}...{{ end }}. Wrap entire resources. Use eq, ne, lt, gt, and, or, not for comparisons. Resource-level conditionals are standard practice.

Q7
What is an umbrella chart?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

An umbrella chart wraps multiple related sub-apps as dependencies. It's a meta-chart that deploys a complete stack (e.g., anihpj + postgres + redis + ingress) via one helm install.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Standard install command:
helm install RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE --create-namespace

# Install with values file:
helm install RELEASE ./chart -f values.yaml -n NAMESPACE

# Install with --set overrides:
helm install RELEASE ./chart --set image.tag=v2.0 -n NAMESPACE

# Install with --atomic (auto-rollback on failure):
helm install RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE --atomic --wait --timeout 5m
Q8
How do you import a specific value from a child chart?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Use import-values in the dependency declaration: { child: service.port, parent: pgPort } makes .Values.pgPort available in the parent.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Chart.yaml with dependencies:
dependencies:
  - name: postgresql
    version: "12.x.x"
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
    condition: postgresql.enabled
  - name: redis
    version: "~18.0.0"
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
    tags:
      - cache

# After adding deps, always run:
helm dependency update
# Downloads .tgz to charts/ and creates Chart.lock

# Then install (dependencies auto-included):
helm install myapp ./chart -n prod
Q9
What files does helm dependency update create/modify?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

It downloads .tgz files into charts/ and creates/updates Chart.lock with exact versions and SHA digests.

Explanation

Dependencies in Chart.yaml are resolved by helm dependency update, which downloads charts to charts/ and creates Chart.lock. Always commit Chart.lock for reproducible builds.

Q10
Should charts/ and Chart.lock be committed to Git?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Chart.lock: YES — always commit. charts/: It depends. Commit for offline builds; .gitignore for clean repos (CI runs helm dependency build). Both approaches are valid.

Explanation

Chart.lock pins exact dependency versions and digests. Always commit to Git for reproducible builds. Rebuild with helm dependency build (no network, faster, reads lock file).

Chapter 10: Hooks & Lifecycle Management

Hooks give you control over when things happen during a Helm operation. Need to run a database migration before upgrading? Back up data before deleting? Hooks let you inject Jobs and other resources at specific points in the release lifecycle.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🪝 Hooks 🎯 20% Exam Weight

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand what Helm Hooks are and when to use them
  • ✅ Master all 8 hook types (pre/post-install, upgrade, delete, rollback, test)
  • ✅ Control hook execution with policies and weights
  • ✅ Create Job-based hooks for database migrations and backups
  • ✅ Build a real DB migration hook for anihpj
Helm Install Lifecycle with Hooks
  helm install myapp ./chart
       │
       ▼
  ┌─────────────────┐
  │ pre-install     │  ← Hook: Job/ConfigMap (weight: -5)
  │ (run DB backup) │
  └────────┬────────┘
           ▼
  ┌─────────────────┐
  │ Render & Apply  │  ← All non-hook resources
  │ K8s Manifests   │    (Deployment, Service, ConfigMap...)
  └────────┬────────┘
           ▼
  ┌─────────────────┐
  │ post-install    │  ← Hook: Job (weight: 5)
  │ (run DB migrate)│
  └────────┬────────┘
           ▼
  ┌─────────────────┐
  │ test            │  ← helm test (test pods)
  │ (verify app)    │
  └─────────────────┘

  HOOK TYPES: pre-install, post-install, pre-delete,
              post-delete, pre-upgrade, post-upgrade,
              pre-rollback, post-rollback, test

  WEIGHTS: Lower numbers run FIRST (-5 before 0 before 5)
  DELETION: hook-succeeded, hook-failed, before-hook-creation

10.1 What are Helm Hooks? — Pre/Post Operations

A Hook is a Kubernetes resource (usually a Job) annotated with "helm.sh/hook": <hook-type>. Instead of being deployed as part of the normal release, hooks run at specific lifecycle events — before install, after upgrade, before delete, etc.

10.2 Hook Types — All 8 Variants

📥
pre-install

Runs BEFORE resources are created. Use for: init scripts, DB schema setup.

✅
post-install

Runs AFTER all resources are created. Use for: data seeding, notifications.

🔄
pre-upgrade

Runs BEFORE upgrade applies. Use for: DB backups, pre-migration checks.

📤
post-upgrade

Runs AFTER upgrade completes. Use for: DB migrations, cache warming.

🗑️
pre-delete

Runs BEFORE resources are deleted. Use for: graceful shutdown, data export.

🧹
post-delete

Runs AFTER deletion. Use for: cleanup external resources.

⏪
pre-rollback

Runs BEFORE rollback. Use for: compatibility checks.

🔙
post-rollback

Runs AFTER rollback. Use for: notification, validation.

10.3 Hook Execution Policy — Controlling Deletion & Failure Behavior

PolicyBehavior
hook-succeededDelete hook resource AFTER it succeeds (default for Jobs)
hook-failedDelete hook resource if it FAILS
before-hook-creationDelete previous hook BEFORE creating new one (default)

10.4 Hook Weights — Controlling Execution Order

Multiple hooks of the same type run in weight order (lowest first). Default weight is 0. Negative weights run before positives.

Hook Weight Example
# Backup runs FIRST (weight: -5), then Migration (weight: 5)
annotations:
  "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade
  "helm.sh/hook-weight": "-5"    # Backup Job
---
annotations:
  "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade
  "helm.sh/hook-weight": "5"     # Migration Job

10.5 Job-Based Hooks — Running Batch Operations

Hook Job Template
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-db-migrate
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "5"
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: migrate
        image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
        command: ["python", "manage.py", "migrate"]

10.6 anihpj DB Migration Hook — Pre-Upgrade Migration Job

Here's a complete, real-world hook for running Django database migrations before every upgrade of anihpj:

templates/db-migrate-hook.yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: {{ include "anihpj.fullname" . }}-db-migrate
  labels: {{ include "anihpj.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "5"
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded,before-hook-creation
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: migrate
        image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
        command: ["python", "manage.py", "migrate", "--noinput"]
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: {{ include "anihpj.fullname" . }}-config
        - secretRef:
            name: {{ include "anihpj.fullname" . }}-secret
🪝HooksLifecycle operations
⚖️WeightsExecution ordering
📋PoliciesDeletion control
🏗️JobsBatch operations
🔄MigrationsDB schema updates
🧪TestOn-demand validation

🪝 Common Hook Patterns & When to Use Each

Hook Decision Flowchart — Which Hook Do I Need?
  Need to run something BEFORE resources are created?
  ──YES──▶ pre-install (init scripts, schema setup)

  Need to run something AFTER resources are created?
  ──YES──▶ post-install (data seeding, notifications)

  Need to run BEFORE an upgrade takes effect?
  ──YES──▶ pre-upgrade (DB backup, compatibility check)

  Need to run AFTER an upgrade completes?
  ──YES──▶ post-upgrade (DB migration, cache warming, smoke tests)

  Need to clean up BEFORE resources are deleted?
  ──YES──▶ pre-delete (data export, deregister from load balancer)

  Need to validate the deployment works?
  ──YES──▶ test (connectivity check, API endpoint test)

  🔑 KEY: Hooks run SYNCHRONOUSLY — they block the release until complete!
     Use --timeout to prevent hung hooks from blocking forever.
⚠️ Hook Timeout Warning

If a hook hangs (e.g., a migration Job can't connect to the DB), it blocks the entire release operation. Always set --timeout on install/upgrade commands. The default timeout is 5 minutes — long enough for most operations, but adjust for large migrations.

10.7 Hook Weights - Controlling Execution Order

When multiple hooks of the same type exist, weights determine execution order. Lower weights run FIRST. The default weight is 0. Weights can be negative or positive.

Hook Weight Execution Order
WEIGHT:  -10           -5            0             5             10
         |              |             |             |              |
pre-install:  [init-secret]  [create-ns]  [default-job]  [migrate-db]  [seed-data]
                (runs first)                                  (runs last)

SAME WEIGHT hooks execute in an undefined order (don't rely on it!)
Use different weights to guarantee ordering.
EXAM
Exam Scenario: "You need to run a DB backup (Job A), then a schema migration (Job B), then a data seed (Job C) before installing the app. How do you ensure order?" Answer: Use pre-install hooks with weights: Job A weight=-10, Job B weight=-5, Job C weight=0. The exam tests weight ordering frequently.

10.8 Hook Deletion Policies - Cleanup Strategies

PolicyWhen Resource is DeletedUse Case
before-hook-creationBefore a new hook of the same type runsReplacing temporary resources; default for most hooks
hook-succeededAfter the hook resource completes successfullyOne-time migration jobs; cleanup after success
hook-failedAfter the hook resource failsLeave failed resources for debugging; auto-cleanup on success
 
# Hook with deletion policy:
metadata:
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "5"
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded, before-hook-creation
    # Multiple policies can be combined with commas

# This means: Delete on success AND delete before next hook of same type
GOTCHA
Resource Lifecycle: Hooks are NOT managed as part of the release. They are NOT updated during helm upgrade unless the hook resource definition changes. If you change a hook's template, Helm will re-create the hook resource on the next operation.

10.9 Hook Failure Handling & Timeouts

Hook Failure Behavior
  • If a hook fails, the entire operation (install/upgrade/delete) fails
  • Failed hooks are NOT automatically retried
  • Use --timeout to set hook timeout (default: 5 min)
  • Hooks can be Jobs or Pods — Jobs are recommended (restartPolicy: Never)
Debugging Failed Hooks
# Check hook status:
kubectl get jobs -l helm.sh/hook
kubectl logs job/hook-job-name

# Check hook events:
kubectl describe job/hook-job-name

# Force re-run by deleting hook resource:
kubectl delete job/hook-job-name
helm upgrade myapp ./chart  # Re-creates hook

# See hook errors in release:
helm status myapp

10.12 The Complete Hook Lifecycle — Step by Step (from Official Docs)

The official Helm documentation defines the exact 13-step lifecycle for a helm install with hooks. Understanding this precise sequence is critical for debugging hook-related issues.

1
User runs helm install

helm install foo ./chart — The Helm client sends the install request to the Helm library (SDK).

2
Helm library install API is called

The SDK's install function is invoked with the chart, values, and options.

3
CRDs in crds/ directory are installed

Any Custom Resource Definitions in the crds/ directory are applied FIRST, before any templates are rendered. CRDs are NOT managed as part of the release — they're never updated or deleted by Helm.

4
Templates are rendered

After verification, the library renders all templates in templates/ (except _*.tpl helper files and NOTES.txt).

5
Pre-install hooks are prepared

The library identifies all resources with helm.sh/hook: pre-install annotation and loads them into Kubernetes.

6
Hooks are sorted by weight

Default weight is 0. Sorted by weight (ascending), then by resource kind, then by name. Lower weights execute FIRST.

7
Lowest-weight hook is loaded

The hook with the lowest weight (most negative) is applied to Kubernetes first.

8
Helm waits until the hook is "Ready"

For Jobs/Pods: wait until successful completion (exit 0). For other resources: wait until Kubernetes marks them as loaded. If ANY hook fails, the ENTIRE install fails.

9
Non-hook resources are loaded

After all pre-install hooks succeed, the actual release resources (Deployments, Services, etc.) are applied to Kubernetes. If --wait is set, Helm waits for all resources to be ready before proceeding.

10
Post-install hooks are prepared

Resources with helm.sh/hook: post-install are identified.

11
Post-install hooks execute

Post-install hooks run (sorted by weight). These run AFTER all release resources are deployed and ready (if --wait).

12
Release object is returned

The library returns the release object (metadata, status, notes) to the Helm client.

13
Client exits

helm install completes. The release is now in deployed state (or failed if any hook or resource failed).

💡
Exam Relevance: Understanding this 13-step process helps you answer questions like: "When does a pre-install hook run?" (step 7-8, before any resources). "Why did my hook fail?" (step 8 — check hook logs). "Can I have multiple hooks of the same type?" (yes, step 6 — they're sorted by weight).

10.13 Hook Patterns for Rollback Operations

Rollback hooks are often overlooked but critical for data integrity. They run during helm rollback and can save you from data corruption.

⏪
Pre-Rollback: Backup Current State
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-pre-rollback-backup
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-rollback
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "-10"
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: backup
        image: postgres:15
        command: ["pg_dump", "-h", "{{ .Release.Name }}-postgresql",
                  "-U", "anihpj", "-f", "/backup/pre-rollback-{{ .Release.Revision }}.sql"]
🔄
Post-Rollback: Verify & Restore
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-post-rollback-verify
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": post-rollback
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "5"
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: verify
        image: anihpj:{{ .Values.image.tag }}
        command: ["python", "manage.py", "check", "--deploy"]
⚠️
Rollback Hook Gotcha: During rollback, Helm creates a NEW revision with the old configuration. Pre-rollback hooks run BEFORE the old resources are restored. Post-rollback hooks run AFTER restoration. The .Release.Revision in the hook template is the NEW revision number, not the target.

10.14 Hook Execution - Concurrency & Parallelism

Hook Execution Model
HOOK EXECUTION ORDER (DEFAULT: SERIAL)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

pre-install hooks:
  [Weight: -10] → Job A runs → completes → Job B starts
  [Weight: -5]  → Job B runs → completes → Job C starts
  [Weight: 0]   → Job C runs → completes
  (ALL hook resources of one weight complete before next weight)

SAME WEIGHT BEHAVIOR:
  [Weight: 0] Job A ──┐
  [Weight: 0] Job B ──┤ Started together (since Helm 3.2+)
  [Weight: 0] Job C ──┘
  (Same-weight hooks can run concurrently)

HOOK TIMEOUT:
  Default: 5 minutes for ALL hooks combined
  Override: --timeout 10m
  Per-hook timeout: NOT supported (use Job's activeDeadlineSeconds)

HOOK FAILURE:
  One hook fails → ENTIRE operation fails
  --atomic: auto-rollback on ANY hook failure
  Failed hooks are preserved for debugging (unless hook-failed policy)

10.15 CRDs and Hooks — Special Handling

Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) have special handling in Helm. They're not hooks — they use the crds/ directory instead.

crds/ Directory (Helm 3+)
  • Files in crds/ are applied BEFORE any templates
  • CRDs are NOT managed as part of the release
  • They are NEVER updated or deleted by Helm
  • No template rendering — they're raw YAML
  • The old crd-install hook was removed in Helm 3
anihpj-chart/
├── crds/
│   └── jobposts.example.com.yaml
├── templates/
│   └── jobpost-cr.yaml  # Uses the CRD
CRD Best Practices
  • Place EXACTLY ONE CRD per file
  • CRDs should be minimal — only what's needed
  • Use a SEPARATE chart for CRDs in production
  • CRDs survive helm uninstall
  • Manual deletion required: kubectl delete crd NAME
# crds/jobposts.example.com.yaml
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: jobposts.anihpj.example.com
spec:
  group: anihpj.example.com
  names:
    kind: JobPost
    plural: jobposts
  scope: Namespaced
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
⚠️
CRD Gotcha: If you upgrade a chart and the CRD template changes, the existing CRD is NOT updated. You must manually apply CRD changes. This prevents accidental breaking changes to custom resources. For production, manage CRDs in a separate Helm chart with its own lifecycle.
Q1
What annotation marks a resource as a Helm hook?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

"helm.sh/hook": <hook-type> (e.g., pre-install, post-upgrade). Jobs are the most common hook resource type.

Explanation

Hooks are regular K8s resources with special annotations. Helm recognizes these annotations and manages the resource differently — running it at lifecycle events instead of deploying it as part of the normal release.

Explanation

Hooks run at lifecycle events via "helm.sh/hook" annotation. Types: pre/post-install/upgrade/delete/rollback, test. Synchronous — block the release. Use weights for ordering and delete policies for cleanup.

Q11
Can a single resource be multiple hook types?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Yes. Use comma-separated values: "helm.sh/hook": post-install,post-upgrade. The resource runs on both events.

Explanation

Multi-hook resources are common for DB migrations (run after install AND upgrade). Each lifecycle event triggers the hook independently. The same template definition is reused across events.

Q12
Do hook resources get deleted during helm uninstall?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

No. Hook resources are NOT managed as part of the release. They persist after uninstall unless they have hook-succeeded or before-hook-creation delete policies. Pre/post-delete hooks are the exception — they run DURING uninstall.

Explanation

Hook resources live independently of the release. Use helm.sh/hook-delete-policy for automatic cleanup, or periodically run kubectl delete job -l helm.sh/hook to clean up completed hook Jobs.

Q13
How do you limit execution time for a hook Job?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Use Kubernetes Job's activeDeadlineSeconds in the hook template spec. If exceeded, the Job is terminated and the hook fails. Different from Helm's --timeout which applies to the entire operation.

Explanation

activeDeadlineSeconds: 300 gives the hook 5 minutes max. Exceeding it causes the entire install/upgrade to fail. Use both: per-hook timeouts via activeDeadlineSeconds, overall operation timeout via --timeout.

Q14
Do hooks have access to .Values and .Release?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Yes. Hooks are regular templates with special annotations. They have FULL access to ALL built-in objects: .Values, .Release, .Chart, .Files, .Capabilities, and .Template.

Explanation

Hooks render at the same time as other templates and share the same context. Use .Values.db.password for migration hooks, .Release.Name for hook resource naming, .Files.Get for SQL migration scripts embedded in the chart.

Q15
What is the difference between hook weight -5 and +5?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

-5 runs FIRST. Lower weights execute before higher weights. Default is 0. Negative = early (backups, pre-checks). Positive = later (notifications, post-processing). Same-weight hooks may run in any order.

Explanation

Weights are strings sorted numerically: -10, -5, 0, +5, +10. Always use distinct weights when ordering matters. The exam may ask you to "ensure Job A runs before Job B" — give Job A a lower (more negative) weight than Job B.

Q2
Name four hook types and when they execute.
Answer & Explanation
Answer

pre-install (before resources created), post-install (after), pre-upgrade (before upgrade), post-upgrade (after). Also: pre-delete, post-delete, pre-rollback, post-rollback, test.

Explanation

Hooks run at lifecycle events via "helm.sh/hook" annotation. Types: pre/post-install/upgrade/delete/rollback, test. Synchronous — block the release. Use weights for ordering and delete policies for cleanup.

Q3
How do you ensure one hook runs before another of the same type?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Use "helm.sh/hook-weight": "<number>". Lower numbers run first. Default is 0. Negative weights run before positives.

Explanation

Hooks run at lifecycle events via "helm.sh/hook" annotation. Types: pre/post-install/upgrade/delete/rollback, test. Synchronous — block the release. Use weights for ordering and delete policies for cleanup.

Q4
What does hook-delete-policy: hook-succeeded do?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Deletes the hook resource (e.g., Job pod) after it completes successfully. Keeps the cluster clean — no lingering completed Job pods.

Explanation

Hooks run at lifecycle events via "helm.sh/hook" annotation. Types: pre/post-install/upgrade/delete/rollback, test. Synchronous — block the release. Use weights for ordering and delete policies for cleanup.

Q5
What resource type is most commonly used for hooks?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Job — it runs a task to completion and exits. ConfigMaps and Secrets can also be hooks but they don't "execute" — they're just created at hook time.

Explanation

Hooks run at lifecycle events via "helm.sh/hook" annotation. Types: pre/post-install/upgrade/delete/rollback, test. Synchronous — block the release. Use weights for ordering and delete policies for cleanup.

Q6
When would you use a pre-upgrade hook?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

For database migrations, backups before schema changes, compatibility checks, or any task that must complete BEFORE the new version goes live.

Explanation

Hooks run at lifecycle events via "helm.sh/hook" annotation. Types: pre/post-install/upgrade/delete/rollback, test. Synchronous — block the release. Use weights for ordering and delete policies for cleanup.

Q7
How are test hooks different from other hooks?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Test hooks run on demand via helm test <release>, not automatically during install/upgrade. They validate the deployment is working correctly.

Explanation

Hooks run at lifecycle events via "helm.sh/hook" annotation. Types: pre/post-install/upgrade/delete/rollback, test. Synchronous — block the release. Use weights for ordering and delete policies for cleanup.

Q8
What annotation controls when a hook resource is deleted?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

"helm.sh/hook-delete-policy". Values: hook-succeeded, hook-failed, before-hook-creation. Multiple policies can be comma-separated.

Explanation

Hooks run at lifecycle events via "helm.sh/hook" annotation. Types: pre/post-install/upgrade/delete/rollback, test. Synchronous — block the release. Use weights for ordering and delete policies for cleanup.

Q9
Why use Jobs instead of Pods for hooks?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Jobs run to completion and track success/failure. Pods just run indefinitely. Jobs are designed for batch operations — exactly what hooks do.

Explanation

Hooks run at lifecycle events via "helm.sh/hook" annotation. Types: pre/post-install/upgrade/delete/rollback, test. Synchronous — block the release. Use weights for ordering and delete policies for cleanup.

Q10
What happens if a hook fails?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

The release operation (install/upgrade/delete) fails and the release enters a failed state. The hook Job pod may remain for debugging. Use --atomic for automatic rollback on failure.

Explanation

Hooks run at lifecycle events via "helm.sh/hook" annotation. Types: pre/post-install/upgrade/delete/rollback, test. Synchronous — block the release. Use weights for ordering and delete policies for cleanup.

Chapter 11: Testing & Validation — Ship with Confidence

Helm provides multiple layers of validation: linting, template rendering, dry-run simulation, schema validation, and test hooks. Together, they form a safety net that catches errors before they reach production. This chapter covers every validation technique.

11.1 Chart Tests — helm test

11.3 helm lint — Catching Template Errors Early

Linting
# Lint a chart
helm lint ./anihpj-chart

# Lint with strict mode (warnings become errors)
helm lint ./anihpj-chart --strict

# Lint with specific values
helm lint ./anihpj-chart -f values-prod.yaml

11.4 helm template — Rendering Without Installing

Template Rendering
# Render templates locally (no cluster needed)
helm template anihpj ./anihpj-chart -f values-prod.yaml

# Render with debug output
helm template anihpj ./anihpj-chart --debug

# Render and validate with kubeval
helm template ./chart | kubeval --strict

11.5 --dry-run — Simulating Install/Upgrade

Dry-Run Simulation
# Simulate install (validates against live cluster)
helm install anihpj-test ./chart --dry-run --debug

# Simulate upgrade
helm upgrade anihpj ./chart --dry-run --debug

# Dry-run is NOT a template render — it talks to the API server
# It validates: API versions, resource types, webhooks

11.7 CI/CD with helm test — Integrating into Pipelines

Lint

2
Template

3
Dry-Run

4
Install

5
Test

6
Cleanup

📊 Validation Methods — Which One When?

MethodSpeedNeeds Cluster?CatchesExam Priority
helm lint⚡ Instant❌ NoSyntax errors, missing required fields, deprecated APIs🔴 ALWAYS FIRST
helm template⚡ Fast❌ NoTemplate rendering errors, missing values, nil pointers🟡 SECOND
--dry-run🐢 Moderate✅ YesAPI version mismatches, webhook rejections, resource conflicts🟢 THIRD
helm test🐢 Slow✅ YesApplication-level issues (connectivity, API responses, DB access)🔵 AFTER DEPLOY
Schema validation⚡ Instant❌ NoInvalid value types, out-of-range values, missing required fields🟡 AUTO
💡 The Validation Pyramid

Run validations in this order: Lint → Template → Dry-Run → Install → Test. Each layer catches different issues. Lint catches 80% of problems before they waste cluster resources. Never skip lint — it takes 1 second and prevents 15 minutes of debugging.

11.8 Test Pod Design Patterns

Well-designed test pods are the difference between catching issues early and debugging production failures. Here are the key patterns:

SMOKE
Smoke Test

Verify the application started and responds. Quick HTTP GET to the service endpoint. Runs fast (~5s).

containers:
- name: smoke-test
  image: curlimages/curl
  command: ["curl", "-f", "http://{{ .Release.Name }}-svc/health"]
INTEG
Integration Test

Verify database connectivity and basic CRUD operations. Takes longer (~30s) but validates the full stack.

containers:
- name: integration-test
  image: anihpj-test:latest
  command: ["./run-tests.sh"]
  env:
  - name: DB_HOST
    value: {{ .Release.Name }}-postgresql

11.9 CI/CD Integration - Automated Testing Workflow

Helm Test in CI/CD Pipeline
GIT PUSH
    |
    v
[1] helm lint ./chart --strict              (1s  - syntax check)
    |
    v
[2] helm template test ./chart --debug      (2s  - render check)
    |
    v
[3] helm install test ./chart --dry-run     (3s  - API validation)
    |
    v
[4] helm install ci-test ./chart -n ci      (30s - actual deploy)
    |
    v
[5] helm test ci-test -n ci --logs          (60s - run test pods)
    |
    v
[6] helm uninstall ci-test -n ci            (10s - cleanup)
    |
    v
[PASS/FAIL]  --  Total time: ~2 minutes per PR
CI/CD Best Practices
  • Always run lint first - catches 80% of issues in 1 second
  • Use dedicated CI namespace - never test in production namespaces
  • Auto-cleanup - uninstall test releases after testing
  • Set timeouts - helm test --timeout 5m prevents hung CI jobs
  • Parallelize - test multiple charts in parallel using different namespaces

11.10 values.schema.json - Advanced Validation

Beyond basic type checking, JSON Schema can enforce complex business rules for chart values.

{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
  "properties": {
    "replicaCount": {
      "type": "integer",
      "minimum": 1,
      "maximum": 100,
      "description": "Number of replicas (1-100)"
    },
    "image": {
      "type": "object",
      "required": ["repository", "tag"],
      "properties": {
        "repository": { "type": "string", "pattern": "^[a-z0-9./-]+$" },
        "tag": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 },
        "pullPolicy": { "enum": ["Always", "IfNotPresent", "Never"] }
      }
    },
    "ingress": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "enabled": { "type": "boolean" },
        "host": { "type": "string", "format": "hostname" }
      },
      "if": { "properties": { "enabled": { "const": true } } },
      "then": { "required": ["host"] }
    }
  },
  "required": ["replicaCount", "image"]
}
GOTCHA
Conditional Validation: The if/then pattern above says: IF ingress.enabled is true, THEN host is required. This prevents users from enabling ingress without specifying a hostname. JSON Schema Draft 7 features like if/then/else and $ref are fully supported in Helm 3.

12.7 OCI-Based Charts - The Modern Standard

Since Helm 3.8.0, OCI (Open Container Initiative) registries are the recommended way to store and distribute Helm charts. This means charts live alongside container images in the same registry.

OCI Workflow
# Login to OCI registry:
helm registry login myregistry.io \
  --username myuser --password mypass

# Package the chart:
helm package ./anihpj-chart

# Push to OCI registry:
helm push anihpj-0.1.0.tgz \
  oci://myregistry.io/helm-charts

# Pull from OCI registry:
helm pull oci://myregistry.io/helm-charts/anihpj \
  --version 0.1.0

# Install directly from OCI:
helm install anihpj \
  oci://myregistry.io/helm-charts/anihpj \
  --version 0.1.0
OCI vs Traditional Repos
FeatureOCITraditional
StorageAny OCI registryHTTP server + index.yaml
AuthRegistry-nativeBasic auth / TLS
VersioningOCI tagsSemVer in index
Toolinghelm push/pullhelm repo add/index

12.8 Chart Signing & Provenance Verification

Chart Signing Workflow
CHART AUTHOR                                CHART CONSUMER
+---------------------+                    +---------------------+
| 1. Generate keypair |                    | 1. Import public key|
|    helm gpg gen key  |                    |    gpg --import key |
+----------+----------+                    +----------+----------+
           |                                          |
           v                                          v
+---------------------+                    +---------------------+
| 2. Package + Sign   |                    | 2. Verify signature |
|    helm package      |                    |    helm verify       |
|    --sign --key '..' | ---- .tgz.prov -->|    chart-0.1.0.tgz  |
|    --keyring ~/.gnupg|                    |    --keyring pubring |
+---------------------+                    +---------------------+

helm package --sign produces: chart-0.1.0.tgz + chart-0.1.0.tgz.prov
The .prov file is a detached signature (OpenPGP clearsigned)
EXAM
Provenance on the Exam: You may be asked to verify a chart's integrity. Remember: helm verify checks the provenance file. helm install --verify does verification during installation. The keyring path must be correct.

12.9 Private Repository Setup - ChartMuseum & Harbor

MUSEUM
ChartMuseum

Lightweight, open-source Helm chart repository server. Supports multiple storage backends (S3, GCS, Azure, local, Swift). Easy to deploy as a Helm chart itself.

# Deploy ChartMuseum:
helm repo add chartmuseum https://chartmuseum.github.io/charts
helm install chartmuseum chartmuseum/chartmuseum \
  --set env.open.DISABLE_API=false
HARBOR
Harbor

Enterprise-grade container + Helm chart registry. Built-in RBAC, vulnerability scanning, replication, and OCI support. CNCF Graduated project.

# Add Harbor as Helm repo:
helm repo add harbor https://harbor.mycompany.com/chartrepo/library \
  --username admin --password xxx

# Or use OCI:
helm registry login harbor.mycompany.com
helm push chart.tgz oci://harbor.mycompany.com/library

11.11 The Testing Pyramid for Helm Charts

Just like software testing, Helm chart validation has layers. Each layer catches different types of errors at different speeds. Running only one layer leaves gaps.

Helm Testing Pyramid
HELM TESTING PYRAMID (Fastest → Most Thorough)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

                    ┌─────┐
                    │ E2E │  helm test (real cluster, real data)
                    │     │  SLOW (30-120s) - Catches: integration, connectivity
                    ├─────┤
                    │DRY  │  helm install --dry-run --debug
                    │RUN  │  MEDIUM (3-5s) - Catches: API validation, K8s errors
                    ├─────┤
                    │TMPL │  helm template --debug
                    │     │  FAST (1-2s) - Catches: render errors, nil pointers
                    ├─────┤
                    │LINT │  helm lint --strict
                    │     │  INSTANT (<1s) - Catches: YAML syntax, missing fields
                    └─────┘

EVERY CI PIPELINE SHOULD RUN ALL FOUR LAYERS IN ORDER.
If lint fails, stop — don't waste time on template/dry-run.
If template fails, stop — don't waste time on dry-run.
If dry-run fails, stop — don't waste time on helm test.

11.12 Understanding helm test Internals

1
Test Discovery

Helm looks for resources annotated with helm.sh/hook: test in the release's stored manifest. These were deployed during install/upgrade but are NOT normal resources — they're hook resources.

2
Test Execution

Tests run in weight order (like other hooks). Each test pod/job is created, and Helm waits for it to complete successfully (exit code 0). Tests can be pods (run once) or jobs (restartPolicy: Never).

3
Result Collection

Helm collects exit codes and logs from each test resource. helm test --logs prints logs even for successful tests. Failed tests show the error output automatically.

4
Test Cleanup

Tests with helm.sh/hook-delete-policy: hook-succeeded are deleted after passing. Failed tests are preserved for debugging. You can re-run tests anytime with helm test — they execute against the current release state.

⚠️
Test Gotcha: Tests run against the LIVE cluster, not a sandbox. A bad test can corrupt data. Always ensure test pods have appropriate RBAC and resource limits. Test pods should be read-only (no mutations) unless explicitly testing write operations.
Q1
What command runs chart tests for a deployed release?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

helm test <release> -n <namespace>. This executes all test hook resources (usually test pods). Use --logs to see output.

Explanation

Test hooks are annotated with "helm.sh/hook": test. They run on demand, not automatically. This separates validation from deployment — you deploy first, then test. 

# Test hook pod template:
metadata:
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": test           # Only runs with helm test
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": before-hook-creation
spec:
  containers:
  - name: test
    command: ["curl", "http://myapp-service/smoke"]
  restartPolicy: Never

# Test command: helm test my-release -n prod --logs

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Standard install command:
helm install RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE --create-namespace

# Install with values file:
helm install RELEASE ./chart -f values.yaml -n NAMESPACE

# Install with --set overrides:
helm install RELEASE ./chart --set image.tag=v2.0 -n NAMESPACE

# Install with --atomic (auto-rollback on failure):
helm install RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE --atomic --wait --timeout 5m
Q2
What's the difference between helm lint and helm template?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

helm lint checks Chart.yaml syntax and template rendering without producing output. helm template renders templates to YAML locally. Lint = validate, Template = render.

Explanation

helm lint catches syntax errors, missing fields, and deprecated APIs. Run it FIRST — a 1-second lint saves 15 minutes of debugging. Use --strict to treat warnings as errors.

Q3
How does --dry-run differ from helm template?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

helm template renders locally (offline). --dry-run connects to the K8s API server and validates API versions, resource types, and admission webhooks — but doesn't create anything.

Explanation

helm template renders YAML locally without a cluster. Unlike --dry-run, it skips API validation. Use --debug for detailed output. Ideal for CI/CD and offline development.

Q4
Where are test pod definitions typically placed?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

In templates/tests/. Common test files: test-connection.yaml (HTTP check), test-db.yaml (database connectivity).

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Minimal valid Chart.yaml:

name: mychart
version: 0.1.0
type: application

# Full Chart.yaml reference:
apiVersion: v2
name: anihpj
version: 0.2.0
appVersion: "2.1.0"
description: A Helm chart for the anihpj job board application
type: application
kubeVersion: ">=1.25.0-0"

  - name: DevOps Team
    email: devops@example.com
icon: https://example.com/anihpj-icon.svg

  - django
  - job-board
  - python
Q5
What JSON Schema keyword ensures a value is within a range?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

"minimum" and "maximum" for numbers. "minLength" and "maxLength" for strings. "enum" for restricted choices.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Key exam commands to remember:
helm lint ./chart --strict
helm template test ./chart --debug
helm install test ./chart --dry-run --debug
helm install prod ./chart -f values.yaml -n NAMESPACE --atomic --wait
helm list -A
helm history RELEASE -n NAMESPACE
helm get manifest RELEASE -n NAMESPACE
helm rollback RELEASE -n NAMESPACE
helm test RELEASE -n NAMESPACE --logs
Q6
What makes a Pod a test pod?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

The annotation "helm.sh/hook": test. This tells Helm to run this pod only when helm test is executed, not during normal install/upgrade.

Explanation

values.schema.json validates user values at install/upgrade time. Key keywords: type, required, enum, minimum/maximum, pattern. Catches invalid config before reaching the cluster.

Q7
How do you validate values against values.schema.json?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Helm automatically validates values against values.schema.json at install/upgrade time. You can also run helm lint which triggers schema validation.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Hook annotations on a Job resource:
metadata:
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade          # Hook type
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "-5"          # Execution order
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded

# Available hook types:
# pre-install, post-install, pre-upgrade, post-upgrade,
# pre-delete, post-delete, pre-rollback, post-rollback, test

# Weights: Lower numbers execute FIRST
# Deletion policies: hook-succeeded, hook-failed, before-hook-creation
Q8
What CI/CD step should come first: lint, template, or dry-run?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Lint (fastest, catches syntax errors) → Template (render locally) → Dry-run (validate against cluster) → Install (deploy) → Test (verify).

Explanation

--dry-run simulates without creating resources. Validates API versions and webhooks against the cluster. Always use before deploying — catches 80% of errors in 2 seconds.

Q9
Can you run helm template without a Kubernetes cluster?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Yes. helm template is purely local — it renders templates to YAML without any cluster connection. Great for CI/CD and offline development.

Explanation

--dry-run simulates without creating resources. Validates API versions and webhooks against the cluster. Always use before deploying — catches 80% of errors in 2 seconds.

Q10
What flag shows test pod logs?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

helm test <release> --logs. This streams test pod output so you can see what passed or failed and why.

Explanation

helm template renders YAML locally without a cluster. Unlike --dry-run, it skips API validation. Use --debug for detailed output. Ideal for CI/CD and offline development.

12.2 Creating Your Own Chart Repository

🏛️
ChartMuseum

Lightweight, open-source Helm chart repository server. Supports S3, GCS, Azure, and local storage. Simple HTTP API for pushing charts.

🏗️
Harbor

Enterprise-grade container + Helm chart registry. Built-in RBAC, vulnerability scanning, replication, and OCI support.

☁️
OCI Registries

Use any OCI-compliant registry (Docker Hub, ECR, ACR, GCR) to store Helm charts. No separate chart server needed!

12.3 OCI-Based Charts — helm push to Container Registry

Helm 3.8+ supports OCI registries natively. Store charts alongside container images in the same registry — simpler infrastructure.

OCI Chart Operations
# Login to OCI registry
helm registry login registry.example.com -u myuser -p mypass

# Package and push
helm package ./anihpj-chart
helm push anihpj-0.1.0.tgz oci://registry.example.com/charts

# Pull from OCI
helm pull oci://registry.example.com/charts/anihpj --version 0.1.0

# Install directly from OCI
helm install anihpj oci://registry.example.com/charts/anihpj --version 0.1.0

# List tags
helm show chart oci://registry.example.com/charts/anihpj
💡 OCI = Simpler Infrastructure

With OCI support, you don't need a separate chart repository server. Your existing container registry (Docker Hub, ECR, ACR, GCR) now stores both images AND charts — one less service to manage.

12.4 Chart Signing & Provenance — helm package --sign

Signing Charts
# Generate a GPG key (one-time)
gpg --full-generate-key

# Package and sign
helm package ./anihpj-chart --sign --key 'devops@anihpj.com' --keyring ~/.gnupg/secring.gpg

# Verify a signed chart
helm verify anihpj-0.1.0.tgz
# Output: Signed by: DevOps Team

12.5 Private Repositories — Authentication & Access Control

Private Repository Auth
# Add private repo with basic auth
helm repo add myprivate https://charts.mycompany.com --username admin --password secret

# Add repo with username prompt (safer)
helm repo add myprivate https://charts.mycompany.com --username admin
# Helm will prompt for the password

# OCI registry login
helm registry login myregistry.azurecr.io -u myuser -p mytoken

12.6 Chart Version Management & Rollout Strategies

📌
Semantic Versioning

Follow MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Bump MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for new features, PATCH for fixes.

🔄
Canary Releases

Deploy new chart version to a subset of users first. Monitor metrics, then promote. helm install canary ./chart --set canary.enabled=true

🔙
Rollback Ready

Every release is versioned. helm rollback restores any previous version in seconds. Keep --history-max high enough.

🌐Public ReposBitnami, Artifact Hub
🏛️Private ReposChartMuseum, Harbor
📦OCIContainer registries
🔏SigningGPG provenance
🔐AuthPrivate repo access

Repository Decision Tree
  Need to share charts publicly?
  ──YES──▶ Artifact Hub (list your repo there)
  │
  NO — Internal/private charts?
  │

  │
  ├── Need enterprise features (RBAC, scanning, replication)?
  │   ──YES──▶ Harbor — full-featured registry for containers + charts.
  │
  └── Need something lightweight and simple?

12.12 Air-Gapped & Offline Environments

1
Download Charts for Offline Use
# Download chart + dependencies to local .tgz:
helm pull bitnami/postgresql --version 12.1.0 --destination ./offline-charts/

# Download with all dependencies:
helm pull bitnami/postgresql --version 12.1.0 --untar
cd postgresql && helm dependency update
cd .. && helm package postgresql
2
Set Up Local Repository
# Create index for local charts:
helm repo index ./offline-charts/

# Serve with any HTTP server:
python3 -m http.server 8080 --directory ./offline-charts/

# Add to Helm:
helm repo add local http://localhost:8080
helm install myapp local/mychart
3
Use OCI for Air-Gapped
# Push to internal OCI registry:

# Pull and install:

12.13 Traditional HTTP vs OCI Repository - Architecture Comparison

Understanding the underlying architecture helps you choose the right repository type and debug connection issues.

Traditional HTTP Repository
ARCHITECTURE:
+--------+     +------------+     +----------+
| Helm   |────>| HTTP Server|────>| Storage  |
| CLI    |     | (nginx, S3)|     | (.tgz    |
+--------+     +------------+     |  files)  |
                                  +----------+

KEY FILE: index.yaml
- Lists all charts + versions
- Contains URLs + SHA256 digests
- Downloaded on helm repo update
- Cached locally at ~/.cache/helm

COMMANDS:
helm repo add NAME URL
helm repo update
helm search repo NAME
helm pull REPO/CHART --version X
OCI-Based Repository
ARCHITECTURE:
+--------+     +------------+     +----------+
| Helm   |────>| OCI        |────>| Blob     |
| CLI    |     | Registry   |     | Storage  |
+--------+     | (Docker,   |     +----------+
               | Harbor,    |
               | ECR, GCR)  |
               +------------+

KEY CONCEPT: Charts as OCI artifacts
- Charts stored as OCI manifests
- Tags used for versioning
- Same auth as Docker (docker login)
- No index.yaml - registry API for listing

COMMANDS:
helm registry login REGISTRY
helm push FILE.tgz oci://REGISTRY/REPO
helm pull oci://REGISTRY/REPO/CHART --version X
helm show chart oci://REGISTRY/REPO/CHART --version X
💡
OCI is the Future: The Helm project recommends OCI for new chart repositories. OCI registries provide better security (built-in auth, RBAC), immutability (digest-based), and integration with existing container infrastructure. Traditional HTTP repos are still supported but no longer the recommended approach.

12.14 Repository Security & Authentication Patterns

🔐
Authenticated Repositories
# HTTP Basic Auth:
helm repo add private https://charts.company.com \
  --username myuser --password mypass

# Token-based (Bearer):
helm repo add private https://charts.company.com \
  --username token --password "$GITLAB_TOKEN"

# TLS Client Certificates:
helm repo add secure https://charts.secure.com \
  --cert-file client.crt \
  --key-file client.key \
  --ca-file ca.crt
🪞
Repository Mirroring
# Mirror a public repo to private:
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
helm repo update

# Pull ALL charts for mirroring:
for chart in $(helm search repo bitnami -l -o json | jq -r '.[].name'); do
  helm pull $chart --destination ./mirror/
done

# Create local index:
helm repo index ./mirror/
# Host via nginx/S3/internal registry

Chapter 13: Security Best Practices

Security in Helm spans RBAC permissions, secrets handling, value protection, provenance verification, network policies, and vulnerability scanning. A single misconfigured chart can expose your entire cluster. This chapter builds your security mindset.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🔒 Security 🎯 15% Exam Weight

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Configure RBAC for Helm operations with ServiceAccounts and ClusterRoles
  • ✅ Manage secrets with Sealed Secrets, External Secrets Operator, and HashiCorp Vault
  • ✅ Never commit secrets to values.yaml — use secure alternatives
  • ✅ Verify chart authenticity with provenance checks
  • ✅ Apply Network Policies and SecurityContexts for defense in depth
  • ✅ Scan container images in charts for CVEs
🎓 Certification Domains
Production 15% Security CRITICAL

13.1 RBAC for Helm — ServiceAccounts & ClusterRoles

Helm RBAC Example
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: helm-deployer
  namespace: production
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: helm-deployer
  namespace: production
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["secrets", "configmaps", "services", "pods"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "create", "update", "delete"]
- apiGroups: ["apps"]
  resources: ["deployments"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "create", "update", "delete"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: helm-deployer
  namespace: production
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: helm-deployer
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: helm-deployer
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

13.2 Secrets Management — Sealed Secrets, External Secrets, Vault

🔐
Sealed Secrets

Encrypt secrets into a SealedSecret CRD that can be safely committed to Git. Only the cluster controller can decrypt them.

🔗
External Secrets

Sync secrets from external providers (AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault) into Kubernetes Secrets automatically.

🏦
HashiCorp Vault

Enterprise-grade secret management. Inject secrets into pods via sidecar or CSI driver. Integrate with Helm via vault CLI or API.

13.3 Values Security — Never Commit Secrets to values.yaml

Secure Values Workflow
  ❌ WRONG: Secrets in values.yaml          ✅ RIGHT: Secrets via external tools
  ─────────────────────────────             ────────────────────────────────
  values.yaml:                              values.yaml:
    dbPassword: "MySecret123"  ← NO!          dbPassword: ""  ← placeholder
    apiKey: "sk-abc123"       ← NO!           apiKey: ""     ← placeholder
                                            helm install ./chart \
  Committed to Git = exposed!                 --set dbPassword=$(vault read -field=pw secret/db) \
                                              --set apiKey=$(aws secretsmanager get-secret-value ...)

13.4 Chart Provenance Verification — helm verify

Provenance Verification
# Verify chart signature and provenance
helm verify anihpj-0.1.0.tgz

# Install only if verified
helm verify anihpj-0.1.0.tgz && helm install anihpj ./anihpj-0.1.0.tgz

# Check provenance file
tar -xzf anihpj-0.1.0.tgz anihpj/Chart.yaml
cat anihpj-0.1.0.tgz.prov

13.5 Network Policies & SecurityContext

Your chart should include security hardening as a best practice. Add a securityContext to pods and optionally include NetworkPolicy templates.

Security Best Practices in Templates
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 1000
    fsGroup: 2000
  containers:
  - name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]

13.6 CVE Scanning for Chart Images

Scanning Images in Charts
# Scan with Trivy
trivy image anihpj/anihpj:v2.1

# Scan in CI pipeline
helm template ./chart | grep "image:" | awk '{print $2}' | tr -d '"' | while read img; do
  trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL "$img"
done

# Use Harbor's built-in vulnerability scanner
# Harbor automatically scans images pushed to its registry
