✅ Helm Security Checklist — Production Readiness

1️⃣
Use dedicated ServiceAccounts

Never use default SA for Helm. Create a dedicated SA with minimal RBAC permissions. Scope to specific namespaces.

2️⃣
Externalize secrets

Use Sealed Secrets, External Secrets Operator, or Vault. Never commit plaintext secrets to Git. Override at deploy time via CI/CD.

3️⃣
Verify chart provenance

Run helm verify before installing any chart from external sources. Only install signed charts in production.

4️⃣
Harden pod security

Set runAsNonRoot: true, drop ALL capabilities, use readOnlyRootFilesystem. Add these to your chart's default values.

5️⃣
Scan images regularly

Integrate Trivy or Harbor scanning in CI/CD. Block deployments with CRITICAL CVEs. Update base images frequently.

6️⃣
Apply Network Policies

Restrict pod-to-pod communication. Only allow necessary ingress/egress. Default-deny with specific allows.

7️⃣
Limit release history

Set --history-max to a reasonable number. Old revisions contain sensitive values. Clean up unused releases.

8️⃣
Use private repositories

Host charts in private OCI registries or Harbor. Authenticate with helm registry login. Never expose internal charts publicly.

13.7 Secrets Management Strategies - Comparison

StrategySecurity LevelComplexityBest For
Sealed SecretsMedium (encrypted, Git-safe)LowGitOps workflows; simple setup
External Secrets OperatorHigh (syncs from vault)MediumAWS/GCP/Azure secrets integration
HashiCorp VaultVery High (dynamic secrets)HighEnterprise; dynamic DB credentials
SOPS + helm-secretsHigh (encrypted values)MediumEncrypted values.yaml files
CI/CD InjectionMedium (pipeline-only)LowSimple setups; --set from CI vars

13.8 Helm-Specific RBAC Patterns

Helm RBAC - Least Privilege Model
MINIMUM PERMISSIONS FOR HELM (per namespace):
=============================================
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: helm-deployer
  namespace: anihpj-prod
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["secrets", "configmaps", "services", "pods"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]
- apiGroups: ["apps"]
  resources: ["deployments", "statefulsets"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]
- apiGroups: ["networking.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["ingresses"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["secrets"]  # For release storage
  verbs: ["get", "list", "create", "update", "delete"]

CI/CD SERVICE ACCOUNT gets helm-deployer Role.
HUMAN OPERATORS get read-only (helm list, helm get) Role.
EMERGENCY ACCESS: Temporary RoleBinding via break-glass process.
GOTCHA
RBAC on the Exam: If Helm can't create Secrets in the release namespace, helm install will fail because Helm 3 stores release info in Secrets. Always grant Secret read/write permissions in the target namespace for the Helm service account.

13.9 Image Vulnerability Scanning for Helm Charts

1
Scan Chart Images

Use Trivy, Grype, or Snyk to scan all container images referenced in your chart's values.yaml and templates.

# Scan all images in a chart:
helm template ./chart | grep 'image:' | awk '{print $2}' | tr -d '"' | \
  xargs -I {} trivy image {}
2
Enforce Policy

Use OPA/Gatekeeper or Kyverno to block deployments with CRITICAL/HIGH CVEs. Integrate with admission webhooks.

3
Sign Trusted Charts

Only allow installation of charts with valid provenance (helm install --verify). Block unsigned charts in production.

13.10 Pod Security Standards in Helm Charts

🔒
Restricted Security Context
# values.yaml
podSecurityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 1000
  runAsGroup: 3000
  fsGroup: 2000
  seccompProfile:
    type: RuntimeDefault

containerSecurityContext:
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  capabilities:
    drop:
    - ALL
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
  runAsNonRoot: true
🛡️
Template Usage
# templates/deployment.yaml
spec:
  securityContext:
    {{- toYaml .Values.podSecurityContext | nindent 4 }}
  containers:
  - name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
    securityContext:
      {{- toYaml .Values.containerSecurityContext | nindent 6 }}
💡
Security on the Exam: Questions may ask you to "ensure the pod runs as non-root" or "drop all capabilities." The answer is always in the securityContext. Include sensible defaults in values.yaml and use toYaml in templates.

13.11 Chart Supply Chain Security

1
Sign Charts

Use GPG/PGP to sign charts. The .prov file is a detached signature that proves authenticity.

helm package --sign --key 'mykey' --keyring ~/.gnupg/secring.gpg ./chart
# Produces: chart-0.1.0.tgz + chart-0.1.0.tgz.prov
2
Verify Before Install
helm verify chart-0.1.0.tgz --keyring ~/.gnupg/pubring.gpg
helm install --verify myapp chart-0.1.0.tgz
# Fails if signature is invalid or missing
3
Scan Images in Charts
# Extract all images from a chart:
helm template ./chart | grep 'image:' | awk '{print $2}' | tr -d '"'
# Scan each with Trivy:
trivy image nginx:1.25

13.12 Network Policies for Helm-Deployed Applications

Helm can deploy NetworkPolicies alongside your application to enforce zero-trust networking. This is a critical production security practice often tested on the exam.

# templates/networkpolicy.yaml
{{ if .Values.networkPolicy.enabled }}
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: {{ include "anihpj.fullname" . }}
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      {{- include "anihpj.selectorLabels" . | nindent 6 }}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: frontend  # Only allow frontend pods
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: {{ .Values.service.port }}
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: postgresql  # Only allow DB egress
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 5432
  - to:  # Allow DNS
    - namespaceSelector: {}
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          k8s-app: kube-dns
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
{{ end }}

13.13 Admission Control Integration

Helm + Admission Controllers Security Pipeline
helm install          kubectl apply        ADMISSION WEBHOOK       K8s API
    |                      |                      |                    |
    v                      v                      v                    v
Rendered YAML ──────> API Request ──────> Validate/Mutate ──────> Apply Resource
                                            |
                              ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
                              │             │             │
                         OPA/Gatekeeper  Kyverno      Pod Security
                         (Rego policies) (CNCF)       Standards
                              │             │             │
                              └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                                            |
                                BLOCK: privilege escalation
                                BLOCK: hostPath volumes
                                BLOCK: runAsRoot containers
                                MUTATE: add resource limits
                                MUTATE: inject sidecars
💡
Exam Insight: Questions about "preventing insecure deployments" should mention admission controllers. Helm alone cannot enforce policy — it generates YAML. Use OPA/Gatekeeper or Kyverno to validate Helm-rendered manifests before they reach the API server.
Q1
What Kubernetes object should you create to give Helm limited deployment permissions?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

A ServiceAccount with a Role (or ClusterRole) and RoleBinding. This limits what Helm can create/delete in the cluster.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Uninstall a release:
helm uninstall RELEASE -n NAMESPACE

# Keep history for potential re-install:
helm uninstall RELEASE -n NAMESPACE --keep-history
# Release status becomes "uninstalled" but history is preserved

# Dry-run uninstall (see what would be deleted):
helm uninstall RELEASE -n NAMESPACE --dry-run

# Cleanup workflow:
helm list -A --failed  # Find failed releases
helm uninstall RELEASE -n NAMESPACE  # Remove them
Q2
Why should you never store secrets in values.yaml?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

values.yaml is plain text and typically committed to Git. Secrets in Git = exposed credentials. Use Sealed Secrets, External Secrets, or Vault instead.

Explanation

values.yaml provides defaults accessed via .Values. Best practices: comment keys, flat nesting, sensible defaults, never store secrets. Override with --set (highest) or -f files.

Q3
What tool can encrypt Kubernetes Secrets for safe Git storage?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Sealed Secrets (Bitnami). Encrypts secrets into SealedSecret CRDs. Only the cluster controller can decrypt. Safe to commit to Git.

Explanation

values.yaml provides defaults accessed via .Values. Best practices: comment keys, flat nesting, sensible defaults, never store secrets. Override with --set (highest) or -f files.

Q4
How do you verify a chart hasn't been tampered with?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

helm verify chart.tgz. This checks the GPG signature and provenance file. Requires the signer's public key in your keyring.

Explanation

Never store plaintext secrets in values.yaml. Use placeholders, inject at deploy time (--set or CI/CD), encode with b64enc in templates. Production: Sealed Secrets, External Secrets Operator, or Vault.

Q5
What securityContext settings make a pod more secure?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

runAsNonRoot: true, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, capabilities.drop: ["ALL"].

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# values.yaml with documented defaults:
replicaCount: 3
image:
  repository: anihpj        # Docker image repository
  tag: v2.0.0                # Image tag (pin in production!)
  pullPolicy: IfNotPresent   # Image pull policy

service:
  type: ClusterIP            # ClusterIP | NodePort | LoadBalancer
  port: 80                   # Service port

ingress:
  enabled: true              # Enable/disable Ingress resource
  className: nginx           # Ingress class name
  host: anihpj.example.com   # Ingress hostname
  tls: true                  # Enable TLS

# Access in templates: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
# Override: --set replicaCount=5
Q6
What tool scans container images for CVEs?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Trivy (Aqua Security) — open-source, fast, comprehensive. Also: Clair, Snyk, and Harbor's built-in scanner.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Key exam commands to remember:
helm lint ./chart --strict
helm template test ./chart --debug
helm install test ./chart --dry-run --debug
helm install prod ./chart -f values.yaml -n NAMESPACE --atomic --wait
helm list -A
helm history RELEASE -n NAMESPACE
helm get manifest RELEASE -n NAMESPACE
helm rollback RELEASE -n NAMESPACE
helm test RELEASE -n NAMESPACE --logs
Q7
How does External Secrets Operator work?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

It syncs secrets from external providers (AWS/GCP/Azure/Vault) into Kubernetes Secrets. Define an ExternalSecret CRD, and the operator keeps K8s Secrets in sync.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# template vs include - Key Difference:

# template: writes directly to output (NO piping)
{{ template "mylib.labels" . }}

# include: returns a string (CAN pipe through functions)
{{ include "mylib.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
{{ include "mylib.labels" . | quote }}

# Named template definition:
{{- define "anihpj.labels" -}}
app.kubernetes.io/name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }}
{{- end }}

# Usage:
metadata:
  labels:
    {{- include "anihpj.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
Q8
What is the principle of least privilege in Helm RBAC?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Give the ServiceAccount only the permissions needed for the chart to work. Don't use cluster-admin. Use namespaced Roles, not ClusterRoles, when possible.

Explanation

Never store plaintext secrets in values.yaml. Use placeholders, inject at deploy time (--set or CI/CD), encode with b64enc in templates. Production: Sealed Secrets, External Secrets Operator, or Vault.

Q9
What file proves a chart was signed by a specific identity?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

The provenance file (.tgz.prov). Generated by helm package --sign. Contains the chart's hash and the signer's digital signature.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# values.yaml with documented defaults:
replicaCount: 3
image:
  repository: anihpj        # Docker image repository
  tag: v2.0.0                # Image tag (pin in production!)
  pullPolicy: IfNotPresent   # Image pull policy

service:
  type: ClusterIP            # ClusterIP | NodePort | LoadBalancer
  port: 80                   # Service port

ingress:
  enabled: true              # Enable/disable Ingress resource
  className: nginx           # Ingress class name
  host: anihpj.example.com   # Ingress hostname
  tls: true                  # Enable TLS

# Access in templates: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
# Override: --set replicaCount=5
Q10
How should you handle secrets in CI/CD pipelines that use Helm?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Inject secrets at deploy time via CI/CD secret variables: helm upgrade --install app ./chart --set dbPassword=$CI_DB_PASSWORD. Never store secrets in the chart repo.

Explanation

Never store plaintext secrets in values.yaml. Use placeholders, inject at deploy time (--set or CI/CD), encode with b64enc in templates. Production: Sealed Secrets, External Secrets Operator, or Vault.

Chapter 14: Helm for CI/CD Pipelines

Helm and CI/CD are a natural fit. Your pipeline builds the container image, packages the chart, pushes to a registry, and deploys to environments — all automated. This chapter covers GitOps with Argo CD, GitHub Actions integration, automated testing, multi-environment strategies, Helmfile, and advanced deployment patterns.

14.1 GitOps with Helm — Argo CD + Helm Integration

Argo CD watches a Git repository for chart changes and automatically syncs them to your cluster. Git is the single source of truth.

Argo CD Application (using Helm)
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: anihpj-prod
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/anihpj/charts
    path: anihpj-chart
    targetRevision: main
    helm:
      valueFiles:
      - values-prod.yaml
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: production
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true

14.2 Helm in GitHub Actions / GitLab CI

GitHub Actions Workflow
name: Deploy with Helm
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v3
    - name: Helm Lint
      run: helm lint ./chart
    - name: Helm Template
      run: helm template test ./chart -f values-prod.yaml
    - name: Deploy to Production
      run: |
        helm upgrade --install anihpj-prod ./chart \
          -f values-prod.yaml \
          -n production --atomic --wait --timeout 10m

14.3 Automated Chart Testing in CI

1
Lint

helm lint ./chart --strict — syntax and best practice validation.

2
Template

helm template test ./chart -f ci-values.yaml — render YAML locally.

3
Install

helm install test ./chart -n ci --create-namespace --atomic

4
Test

helm test test -n ci --logs — run test hooks.

5
Cleanup

helm uninstall test -n ci

14.4 Multi-Environment Deployments with Helm

Multi-Environment Deploy
# Same chart, different values per environment
helm upgrade --install anihpj-dev  ./chart -f values-dev.yaml  -n dev  --atomic --wait
helm upgrade --install anihpj-stg  ./chart -f values-staging.yaml -n staging --atomic --wait
helm upgrade --install anihpj-prod ./chart -f values-prod.yaml -n production --atomic --wait

14.5 Helmfile — Declarative Helm Releases

Helmfile lets you declare all your releases in a single YAML file. Instead of running helm install for each release, you run helmfile apply once.

helmfile.yaml
repositories:
- name: bitnami
  url: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
releases:
- name: anihpj-prod
  namespace: production
  chart: ./anihpj-chart
  values:
  - values-prod.yaml
- name: postgresql
  namespace: production
  chart: bitnami/postgresql
  version: 12.5.0
- name: redis
  namespace: production
  chart: bitnami/redis
  version: 18.0.0

14.6 Blue-Green & Canary Deployments with Helm

🔵🟢
Blue-Green

Deploy new version (green) alongside old (blue). Switch traffic via Service selector. Instant rollback: switch selector back. helm install anihpj-green ./chart --set color=green

🐤
Canary

Gradually shift traffic to new version. Start with 10%, monitor, increase. helm upgrade anihpj-canary ./chart --set canary.weight=10

🔄GitOpsArgo CD + Helm
⚡CI/CDGitHub Actions
🧪TestingAutomated in CI
🏗️Multi-EnvDev → Staging → Prod
📋HelmfileDeclarative releases
🔵🟢StrategiesBlue-Green & Canary

🏭 CI/CD Pipeline Best Practices for Helm

🔒
Never commit secrets to chart repo

Inject secrets at deploy time via CI/CD variables. helm upgrade --install app ./chart --set dbPassword=$CI_SECRET. Values files in Git should contain placeholders, never real secrets.

📦
Version charts automatically

Use CI to auto-increment chart version on merge. Tools like helm-bump or semantic-release can automate SemVer bumps.

🧪
Test in isolated namespaces

Each CI run deploys to a unique namespace: helm install pr-123 ./chart -n ci-pr-123 --create-namespace. Clean up after tests pass. No cross-contamination.

📊
Monitor rollout health

After deploy, wait for rollout: kubectl rollout status deploy/app -n production --timeout=5m. Alert if rollout doesn't complete.

🔙
Auto-rollback on failure

Always use --atomic flag. If deployment fails, Helm auto-rolls back. Add health checks to your templates so failures are detected quickly.

📝
Generate change logs

Use helm diff plugin in CI to show what changed. Post the diff as a PR comment for review before merge. helm diff upgrade app ./chart -f values-prod.yaml

CI/CD Decision Flow for Helm Deployments
  Git Push → PR Opened?
  ──YES──▶ helm lint + helm template (validate) → helm diff (show changes)
  │         → Review diff → Merge → Deploy pipeline
  │
  ──NO (merge to main)──▶
  │
  ▼
  helm lint --strict
  │  FAIL → ❌ Stop pipeline, notify
  ▼
  helm template -f values-prod.yaml
  │  FAIL → ❌ Template error, fix
  ▼
  helm install test ./chart -n ci --dry-run
  │  FAIL → ❌ API validation error
  ▼
  helm upgrade --install prod ./chart -f values-prod.yaml --atomic --wait --timeout 10m
  │  FAIL → Auto-rollback (--atomic), alert team
  ▼
  helm test prod --logs
  │  FAIL → ⚠️ App issue, investigate
  ▼
  🎉 Deployed successfully!
⏱️ 20 minutes
🏋️ Hands-On Drill: Build a Complete CI/CD Pipeline with Helm

Scenario: Set up a CI/CD pipeline that lints, tests, and deploys the anihpj chart to staging, then promotes to production.

  1. Lint: helm lint ./anihpj-chart --strict
  2. Template: helm template test ./anihpj-chart -f values-staging.yaml --debug
  3. Deploy to Staging: helm upgrade --install anihpj-stg ./anihpj-chart -f values-staging.yaml -n staging --create-namespace --atomic --wait
  4. Test: helm test anihpj-stg -n staging --logs
  5. Verify: kubectl get all -n staging and curl the service endpoint
  6. Promote to Production: helm upgrade --install anihpj-prod ./anihpj-chart -f values-prod.yaml -n production --atomic --wait --timeout 10m
  7. Verify Production: helm status anihpj-prod -n production
✅ Complete Pipeline Script 
#!/bin/bash
set -e
CHART="./anihpj-chart"
echo "🔍 Linting..."
helm lint $CHART --strict
echo "📄 Rendering templates..."
helm template test $CHART -f values-staging.yaml --debug > /dev/null
echo "🚀 Deploying to staging..."
helm upgrade --install anihpj-stg $CHART -f values-staging.yaml -n staging --create-namespace --atomic --wait --timeout 5m
echo "🧪 Running tests..."
helm test anihpj-stg -n staging --logs
echo "✅ Staging verified. Promoting to production..."
helm upgrade --install anihpj-prod $CHART -f values-prod.yaml -n production --atomic --wait --timeout 10m
echo "🎉 Production deployed! Status:"
helm status anihpj-prod -n production

14.7 GitOps with Helm + Argo CD

GitOps Workflow - Argo CD + Helm
GIT REPOSITORY                      ARGO CD                      KUBERNETES
+------------------+           +------------------+          +------------------+
| helm-charts/     |           | Argo CD          |          | Production       |
|   anihpj/        |  git pull |                  |  sync    | Cluster          |
|     Chart.yaml   |---------->| Application CRD  |--------->| + namespace: prod|
|     values.yaml  |  (every   |   source:        |  (every  |   anihpj-prod    |
|     values-prod  |   3 min)  |     repoURL: git |   3 min) |   release v3     |
|     templates/   |           |     path: anihpj  |          |                  |
+------------------+           |     targetRev:    |          +------------------+
                               |       main        |
                               +------------------+

ARGOCD APPLICATION YAML:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: anihpj-prod
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/myorg/helm-charts
    targetRevision: main
    path: anihpj
    helm:
      values: |
        replicaCount: 3
        image:
          tag: v2.0.0
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: production
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
EXAM
GitOps Exam Question: "How do you ensure a Helm release stays in sync with its Git repository?" Answer: Use Argo CD or Flux CD with automated sync. The Application CRD watches the Git repo and automatically reconciles the cluster state with the desired state. selfHeal: true detects and fixes manual changes (drift).

14.8 GitHub Actions Pipeline - Complete Example

# .github/workflows/helm-release.yml
name: Helm Chart CI/CD

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ['anihpj-chart/**']

jobs:
  lint-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Setup Helm
        uses: azure/setup-helm@v4
      - name: Setup Kind
        uses: helm/kind-action@v1
      - name: Lint
        run: helm lint ./anihpj-chart --strict
      - name: Template Render
        run: helm template test ./anihpj-chart --debug
      - name: Install + Test
        run: |
          helm install ci-test ./anihpj-chart -n ci --create-namespace --wait
          helm test ci-test -n ci --logs
          helm uninstall ci-test -n ci

  publish:
    needs: lint-test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Package & Push
        run: |
          helm package ./anihpj-chart
          helm registry login ghcr.io -u \${{ github.actor }} -p \${{ secrets.GH_TOKEN }}
          helm push anihpj-*.tgz oci://ghcr.io/\${{ github.repository_owner }}/charts

14.9 Blue-Green & Canary Deployments with Helm

Blue-Green Strategy
# Deploy GREEN (new version):
helm install anihpj-green ./chart \
  --set image.tag=v2.0 \
  --set service.name=anihpj-green \
  -n production

# Test GREEN:
curl http://anihpj-green.production.svc

# Switch traffic to GREEN:
kubectl patch svc anihpj-prod -n production \
  -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"version":"green"}}}'

# Decommission BLUE:
helm uninstall anihpj-blue -n production
Canary Strategy
# Deploy CANARY (10% traffic):
helm install anihpj-canary ./chart \
  --set image.tag=v2.0 \
  --set replicaCount=1 \
  -n production

# Traffic split via Ingress/Service Mesh:
# 90% -> anihpj-stable (v1.0)
# 10% -> anihpj-canary (v2.0)

# Monitor canary for 30 min:
helm test anihpj-canary -n production

# Promote canary to stable:
helm upgrade anihpj-stable ./chart \
  --set image.tag=v2.0 -n production
helm uninstall anihpj-canary -n production
class="cka-exam-questions">
Q1
What is GitOps and how does Helm fit into it?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

GitOps uses Git as the single source of truth. Helm charts are stored in Git. Argo CD or Flux watches the repo and syncs changes to the cluster automatically.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Standard install command:
helm install RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE --create-namespace

# Install with values file:
helm install RELEASE ./chart -f values.yaml -n NAMESPACE

# Install with --set overrides:
helm install RELEASE ./chart --set image.tag=v2.0 -n NAMESPACE

# Install with --atomic (auto-rollback on failure):
helm install RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE --atomic --wait --timeout 5m
Q2
What CI step should run before helm install in a pipeline?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

helm lint (syntax check), then helm template (render YAML), then helm install --dry-run (validate against cluster). All three before actual install.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Standard install command:
helm install RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE --create-namespace

# Install with values file:
helm install RELEASE ./chart -f values.yaml -n NAMESPACE

# Install with --set overrides:
helm install RELEASE ./chart --set image.tag=v2.0 -n NAMESPACE

# Install with --atomic (auto-rollback on failure):
helm install RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE --atomic --wait --timeout 5m
Q3
What is Helmfile?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

A declarative tool for managing multiple Helm releases. Define all releases in helmfile.yaml and apply them with one command: helmfile apply.

Explanation

helm install creates a new release tracked in Kubernetes Secrets. Key flags: --atomic (auto-rollback), --wait (wait for readiness), --dry-run (validate first). Always dry-run before deploying on the exam.

Q4
How do you deploy the same chart to dev, staging, and prod?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Use different values files: helm install app-dev ./chart -f values-dev.yaml -n dev, helm install app-prod ./chart -f values-prod.yaml -n production.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Standard install command:
helm install RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE --create-namespace

# Install with values file:
helm install RELEASE ./chart -f values.yaml -n NAMESPACE

# Install with --set overrides:
helm install RELEASE ./chart --set image.tag=v2.0 -n NAMESPACE

# Install with --atomic (auto-rollback on failure):
helm install RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE --atomic --wait --timeout 5m
Q5
How does Argo CD deploy a Helm chart?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Argo CD reads an Application CRD that points to a Git repo + chart path. It runs helm template and applies the rendered YAML. Git changes trigger automatic sync.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# template vs include - Key Difference:

# template: writes directly to output (NO piping)
{{ template "mylib.labels" . }}

# include: returns a string (CAN pipe through functions)
{{ include "mylib.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
{{ include "mylib.labels" . | quote }}

# Named template definition:
{{- define "anihpj.labels" -}}
app.kubernetes.io/name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }}
{{- end }}

# Usage:
metadata:
  labels:
    {{- include "anihpj.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
Q6
What is the idempotent install/upgrade command for CI/CD?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

helm upgrade --install <release> ./chart -f values.yaml -n <ns> --atomic --wait --timeout 10m. Works whether the release exists or not.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Standard upgrade:
helm upgrade RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE

# Upgrade with new values:
helm upgrade RELEASE ./chart -f values-new.yaml -n NAMESPACE

# Upgrade-or-install (idempotent):
helm upgrade --install RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE

# Upgrade with auto-rollback:
helm upgrade RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE --atomic --cleanup-on-fail
Q7
What's the difference between Blue-Green and Canary deployments?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Blue-Green: two complete environments, switch traffic all at once. Canary: gradually shift a percentage of traffic. Blue-Green = instant rollback. Canary = gradual validation.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Rollback to previous revision:
helm rollback RELEASE -n NAMESPACE

# Rollback to specific revision:
helm rollback RELEASE 3 -n NAMESPACE

# View history first:
helm history RELEASE -n NAMESPACE
# 1  Tue Jan 15 10:00:00 2024  SUPERSEDED  anihpj-0.1.0  1.0.0  Install complete
# 2  Tue Jan 15 10:30:00 2024  SUPERSEDED  anihpj-0.1.1  1.0.1  Upgrade complete
# 3  Tue Jan 15 11:00:00 2024  FAILED      anihpj-0.2.0  2.0.0  Upgrade failed

# Rollback creates a NEW revision:
helm rollback RELEASE 2 -n NAMESPACE
# Creates revision 4 with config from revision 2
Q8
How do you automate chart testing in CI?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Deploy to a temporary CI namespace, run helm test, then uninstall. Lint → Template → Install → Test → Cleanup. All in a pipeline job.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Validate chart structure and syntax:
helm lint ./chart --strict

# Common lint checks:
# - Chart.yaml has required fields (apiVersion, name, version)
# - values.yaml is valid YAML
# - Templates parse without errors
# - Deprecated API versions flagged
# - Missing required values detected

# Debug workflow:
# 1. helm lint --strict     (1 second, catches 80%)
# 2. helm template --debug  (2 seconds, render check)
# 3. helm install --dry-run (3 seconds, API validation)
Q9
When should you use Kustomize instead of Helm?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

For environment-specific overlays on existing YAML (no templating needed). Kustomize patches base YAML without parameters. Helm is better for reusable, parameterized charts.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Key exam commands to remember:
helm lint ./chart --strict
helm template test ./chart --debug
helm install test ./chart --dry-run --debug
helm install prod ./chart -f values.yaml -n NAMESPACE --atomic --wait
helm list -A
helm history RELEASE -n NAMESPACE
helm get manifest RELEASE -n NAMESPACE
helm rollback RELEASE -n NAMESPACE
helm test RELEASE -n NAMESPACE --logs
Q10
What makes --atomic critical for CI/CD pipelines?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

If the upgrade fails, --atomic automatically rolls back to the previous working state. Prevents broken deployments from staying live in production.

Explanation

--atomic auto-rolls back on failure — your safety net. Combine with --wait --timeout. Without it, failed releases stay broken. Essential for production and exam deployments.

The Helm certification is a performance-based exam. Knowing Helm isn't enough — you need speed, accuracy, and a systematic approach. This chapter gives you the complete exam strategy: format, domain breakdown, terminal setup, time management, and the 10 mistakes that cost candidates points.

15.8 Top 10 Mistakes That Cost Points

1️⃣
Not using --dry-run first

Always simulate before deploying. helm install --dry-run catches API errors without polluting the cluster.

2️⃣
Forgetting --namespace

Wrong namespace = 0 points. Read the question carefully for namespace requirements.

3️⃣
Not using helm create

Writing chart structure from scratch wastes time. Always scaffold with helm create.

4️⃣
Skipping helm lint

Deploying without linting is gambling. helm lint takes 1 second and catches syntax errors.

5️⃣
Nil pointer panics in templates

Accessing undefined values crashes templates. Always use default: {{ .Values.x | default "safe" }}.

6️⃣
Wrong value precedence

--set beats -f files. Multiple -f: last wins. Know the precedence chain cold.

7️⃣
Not using helm show values

Need to know what values a chart accepts? helm show values chart prints them all with comments.

8️⃣
Forgetting --atomic on upgrades

Failed upgrade without --atomic leaves release in failed state. Always use --atomic for safety.

9️⃣
Confusing version vs appVersion

version = chart version (templates). appVersion = application version (image). They're different.

🔟
Spending too long on one question

5+ minutes stuck? Flag and move on. Points per minute is the real metric.

15.11 Top 15 Exam Mistakes - Don't Lose Points

#MistakeImpactHow to Avoid
1Forgetting --namespaceDeploying to wrong namespace = 0 pointsAlways use -n flag. Set context namespace.
2Not using --dry-runFailed installs waste timeAlways dry-run before actual install
3Missing --atomicPartial deployments hard to debugUse --atomic --wait for clean rollback
4Wrong values precedenceUnexpected configurationMemorize: --set > -f (last wins) > values.yaml
5Template whitespace errorsInvalid YAML outputUse {{- -}} for whitespace control
6Nil pointer dereferenceTemplate render failsUse default function on ALL nullable values
7Not running helm lintSyntax errors discovered lateLint takes 1 second - always do it first
8Forgetting helm dependency updateMissing subchart dependenciesRun after any Chart.yaml dependency change
9Hook weight conflictsUnpredictable hook executionUse unique weights for each hook
10Wrong SemVer constraintDependency resolution failsUse explicit ranges: >=1.0.0 <2.0.0
11Not saving rendered outputCan't debug failed installsPipe to file: helm template . > out.yaml
12Using template instead of includeCan't pipeline through functionsinclude returns string; template writes directly
13Missing .helmignoreLarge chart packages include junkAlways create .helmignore with node_modules, .git, etc.
14Not testing hooksHook failures block deployTest hooks with helm test before production
15Copy-paste without adaptingWrong namespace/name/valuesAlways review pasted commands before executing

15.12 Mental Models for the Exam

🧠
The Install Decision Tree
Is this a NEW app?
  YES -> helm install NAME ./chart -n NS
  NO  -> Does it need CHANGES?
           YES -> helm upgrade NAME ./chart -n NS
           NO  -> Done!

Did the upgrade FAIL?
  YES -> helm rollback NAME -n NS
  NO  -> Done!

Need to REMOVE?
  YES -> helm uninstall NAME -n NS

Need to CHECK what's deployed?
  -> helm list -A
  -> helm history NAME -n NS
  -> helm get manifest NAME -n NS
🔍
The Debug Decision Tree
Chart won't LINT?
  -> Check Chart.yaml syntax
  -> Check template {{ }} balance
  -> helm lint ./chart --strict

Template won't RENDER?
  -> Check .Values.xxx exists
  -> Add | default "fallback"
  -> helm template ./chart --debug

Install FAILS?
  -> helm install --dry-run --debug
  -> Check namespace exists
  -> Check RBAC permissions

Release DRIFTS?
  -> helm get manifest | kubectl diff -f -
  -> helm upgrade --reuse-values

THE HELM EXAM CHEAT SHEET
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
VALUE PRECEDENCE: --set > -f (last wins) > values.yaml
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
INSTALL:  helm install NAME ./chart -n NS --create-namespace
UPGRADE:  helm upgrade NAME ./chart -n NS --atomic --wait
ROLLBACK: helm rollback NAME [REV] -n NS

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

PUSH OCI: helm push FILE.tgz oci://REGISTRY/REPO

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

include   = returns string (CAN pipe through functions)

required  = error if null/empty
toYaml    = convert object to YAML string

quote     = wrap in double quotes

15.14 The 95%+ Strategy — What Separates Top Scorers

Getting 70-85% is knowing Helm. Getting 95%+ is knowing Helm's traps. Here's what the top 5% do differently.

The 95%+ Mental Model
70-85% SCORER                          95%+ SCORER
═══════════════════════════════════     ═══════════════════════════════════
Reads the question → types command      Reads the question → checks NAMESPACE
                                        FIRST, then types command

helm install app ./chart                helm install app ./chart \
                                          -n EXACT-NAMESPACE-FROM-QUESTION \
                                          --create-namespace --atomic --wait

Uses default values                     Checks if question requires SPECIFIC
                                        values.yaml or --set overrides

helm lint ./chart                       helm lint ./chart --strict --quiet
                                        (--strict treats warnings as errors)

Forgets --dry-run on upgrades           ALWAYS dry-runs before every upgrade
                                        helm upgrade app ./chart --dry-run

Doesn't verify after install            Shows verification commands in answer:

15.15 The 10 Most Common Point-Losing Mistakes (And How to Never Make Them)

#MistakePoints LostThe 95%+ Fix
1Wrong namespace100% of questionRead namespace FIRST. Type -n NS BEFORE the command. Make it the FIRST thing you type.
2Missing --create-namespaceInstall failsAlways add --create-namespace on install. Remove only if the question says "namespace already exists."
3Not using --atomicPartial failuresEvery production install/upgrade gets --atomic --wait. The ONLY exception: the question explicitly says "do not rollback on failure."
4Forgetting --reuse-values vs --reset-valuesWrong configMantra: "New install = use -f file. Upgrade keeping old = --reuse-values. Upgrade fresh = --reset-values -f new-file."
5Not saving answer file immediatelyLost workCopy every successful command to the answer file THE MOMENT it works. Don't wait until the end.
6Spending >5 min on one question5+ missed questionsSet a hard 5-minute timer per question. Flag and skip. Come back with remaining time.
7Editing templates instead of valuesWrong approachIf the question says "change replicas to 5", use --set replicaCount=5 or edit values.yaml. NEVER edit templates/deployment.yaml.
8Not running helm lint firstDebugging wastehelm lint --strict takes 1 second. It catches typos, missing fields, bad YAML. ALWAYS run it before install.
9Leaving failed releases undeletedName conflictsAfter a failed attempt: helm uninstall NAME -n NS then re-try. Failed releases block the name.
10Not verifying after operationsUnnoticed failuresAfter every install/upgrade: helm list -n NS; helm history NAME -n NS; helm status NAME -n NS. Show the examiner you verified.

Answer & Explanation
Answer

helm upgrade --install <name> ./chart -f values.yaml -n <ns> --create-namespace --atomic --wait --timeout 5m. Idempotent (install or upgrade), atomic (auto-rollback), wait (verify readiness). This single command pattern handles 90% of exam deploy tasks.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Standard upgrade:
helm upgrade RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE

# Upgrade with new values:
helm upgrade RELEASE ./chart -f values-new.yaml -n NAMESPACE

# Upgrade-or-install (idempotent):
helm upgrade --install RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE

# Upgrade with auto-rollback:
helm upgrade RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE --atomic --cleanup-on-fail
Q5
The exam asks you to "deploy a chart named webapp to the prod namespace." You run the install but forget --namespace. What happens?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

0 points for that question. The exam scores exact requirements. Wrong namespace = wrong answer, even if the chart deploys perfectly. Always verify with kubectl config view --minify | grep namespace before deploying.

Explanation

On the exam, namespace accuracy is critical. Wrong namespace = 0 points. Always read questions carefully for namespace requirements. Use -n <ns> explicitly. Verify with kubectl config view --minify.

Q6
What's the 3-pass time strategy for the 120-minute exam?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Pass 1 (0-35 min): Quick wins — everything under 3 minutes. Pass 2 (35-90 min): Medium tasks — template writing, value config. Pass 3 (90-120 min): Hard tasks + review flagged questions.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# template vs include - Key Difference:

# template: writes directly to output (NO piping)
{{ template "mylib.labels" . }}

# include: returns a string (CAN pipe through functions)
{{ include "mylib.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
{{ include "mylib.labels" . | quote }}

# Named template definition:
{{- define "anihpj.labels" -}}
app.kubernetes.io/name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }}
{{- end }}

# Usage:
metadata:
  labels:
    {{- include "anihpj.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
Q7
You finish Pass 2 with 20 minutes remaining and 5 flagged questions. What's your priority order?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

1. Answer any completely unattempted questions (even partial answers may earn partial credit). 2. Review flagged questions in order of domain weight (Core > Templates > Advanced > Production). 3. Verify namespace correctness on all answers. 4. Run helm list -A to confirm all expected releases exist.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# List releases in current namespace:
helm list

# List ALL releases across ALL namespaces:
helm list -A

# List only failed releases:
helm list -A --failed

# List releases sorted by date:
helm list -A --date --reverse

# List with specific filter:
helm list -n production --filter anihpj
Q8
Why should you ALWAYS run --dry-run before helm install on the exam?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

--dry-run --debug validates API versions, catches template errors, and shows exactly what would be deployed — without creating anything. A failed install wastes time on cleanup. Dry-run catches 80% of errors in 2 seconds.

Explanation

helm install creates a new release tracked in Kubernetes Secrets. Key flags: --atomic (auto-rollback), --wait (wait for readiness), --dry-run (validate first). Always dry-run before deploying on the exam.

Q9
How should you handle secrets (passwords, API keys) during the exam?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Use --set to inject at deploy time: helm install app ./chart --set db.password=exam123. Never hardcode secrets in values.yaml. For Secret templates, use {{ .Values.secret | b64enc }} to encode at render time.

Explanation

Never store plaintext secrets in values.yaml. Use placeholders, inject at deploy time (--set or CI/CD), encode with b64enc in templates. Production: Sealed Secrets, External Secrets Operator, or Vault.

Q10
With 2 minutes left, what should you verify before submitting?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

1. helm list -A — verify all expected releases are deployed. 2. Check namespace requirements on your 3 hardest questions. 3. Ensure no release is in "failed" state. 4. Submit — don't second-guess yourself in the final seconds.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Standard install command:
helm install RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE --create-namespace

# Install with values file:
helm install RELEASE ./chart -f values.yaml -n NAMESPACE

# Install with --set overrides:
helm install RELEASE ./chart --set image.tag=v2.0 -n NAMESPACE

# Install with --atomic (auto-rollback on failure):
helm install RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE --atomic --wait --timeout 5m

16.6 Lab 6: Multi-Environment Deployment with Values Files (15 min)

1
Create Environment Values Files
# values-dev.yaml
replicaCount: 1
image:
  tag: latest
  pullPolicy: Always
ingress:
  enabled: false
resources:
  limits:
    cpu: 200m
    memory: 256Mi

# values-prod.yaml
replicaCount: 3
image:
  tag: v2.0.0
  pullPolicy: IfNotPresent
ingress:
  enabled: true
  host: anihpj.example.com
resources:
  limits:
    cpu: 1000m
    memory: 1Gi
2
Deploy to Both Environments
helm install anihpj-dev ./anihpj-chart -f values-dev.yaml -n dev --create-namespace
helm install anihpj-prod ./anihpj-chart -f values-prod.yaml -n production --create-namespace
3
Verify Different Configurations
# Check replicas in each env:
kubectl get deploy -n dev anihpj-dev -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}'  # Should be 1
kubectl get deploy -n production anihpj-prod -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}'  # Should be 3

# Check ingress (should only exist in prod):
kubectl get ingress -n dev      # Should be empty
kubectl get ingress -n production  # Should show anihpj-prod

16.7 Lab 7: Hook-Based Database Migration (20 min)

1
Create Migration Hook Template
# templates/hooks/db-migrate.yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-db-migrate
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "-5"
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: migrate
        image: anihpj:{{ .Values.image.tag }}
        command: ["python", "manage.py", "migrate"]
        env:
        - name: DATABASE_URL
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: {{ .Release.Name }}-db-secret
              key: url
2
Test the Migration Hook
# Install initial version:
helm install anihpj ./anihpj-chart -n staging --create-namespace

# Verify hook ran:
kubectl get jobs -n staging -l helm.sh/hook
helm history anihpj -n staging

# Upgrade (triggers pre-upgrade hook):
helm upgrade anihpj ./anihpj-chart --set image.tag=v2.1 -n staging

1
Package and Push to OCI Registry

# Package chart:

# Push to OCI:
helm push anihpj-0.1.0.tgz oci://ghcr.io/YOUR_ORG/helm-charts

# List remote charts:
helm show chart oci://ghcr.io/YOUR_ORG/helm-charts/anihpj --version 0.1.0
2
Install from OCI Registry

helm pull oci://ghcr.io/YOUR_ORG/helm-charts/anihpj --version 0.1.0

# Install directly:
helm install anihpj oci://ghcr.io/YOUR_ORG/helm-charts/anihpj \
  --version 0.1.0 -n production --create-namespace

16.9 Lab 9: Troubleshooting Broken Releases (15 min)

1
Debug a Failed Installation
# Simulate a failure: install with invalid image tag
helm install broken ./anihpj-chart --set image.tag=INVALID_TAG -n debug

# Check status:
helm status broken -n debug
helm history broken -n debug

# Get rendered manifests to find the error:
helm get manifest broken -n debug | grep -A5 image

# Fix and upgrade:
helm upgrade broken ./anihpj-chart --set image.tag=v2.0 -n debug
2
Detect and Fix Release Drift
# Someone manually edited a deployment:
kubectl scale deploy broken-anihpj --replicas=10 -n debug

# Detect drift:
kubectl diff -f <(helm get manifest broken -n debug)

# Fix by re-applying Helm state:
helm upgrade broken ./anihpj-chart --reuse-values -n debug

16.11 Lab 11: Timed 30-Minute Sprint — 10 Tasks (30 min, 10 points each)

This lab is designed to be done AGAINST THE CLOCK. Set a 30-minute timer. No pausing. No looking at answers until time is up. Score yourself honestly. Repeat until you score 90+.

T1
Create & Install (3 min, 10 pts)
# Create a chart named "sprint" and install it as "sprint-dev"
# in namespace "sprint-ns" with 2 replicas
# VERIFICATION: helm list -n sprint-ns shows sprint-dev deployed
helm create sprint
helm install sprint-dev ./sprint --set replicaCount=2 -n sprint-ns --create-namespace --atomic --wait
helm list -n sprint-ns
T2
Values Override (3 min, 10 pts)
# Create values-custom.yaml with service.type=NodePort and service.port=8080
# Upgrade sprint-dev using this file
cat > values-custom.yaml <
T3
Rollback (2 min, 10 pts)
# Rollback sprint-dev to revision 1 and verify
helm rollback sprint-dev 1 -n sprint-ns
helm history sprint-dev -n sprint-ns
# Revision 3 should be DEPLOYED with rev 1 config
T4
Second Environment (3 min, 10 pts)
# Install the same sprint chart as "sprint-prod" in "sprint-prod-ns"
# with 5 replicas and service.type=ClusterIP
helm install sprint-prod ./sprint   --set replicaCount=5 --set service.type=ClusterIP   -n sprint-prod-ns --create-namespace --atomic --wait
helm list -n sprint-prod-ns
T5
Dry-Run & Lint (3 min, 10 pts)
# Lint the sprint chart with --strict, then do a dry-run upgrade
# of sprint-prod with replicaCount=10
helm lint ./sprint --strict
helm upgrade sprint-prod ./sprint --set replicaCount=10   -n sprint-prod-ns --dry-run --debug 2>&1 | head -30
T6
Template Debugging (4 min, 10 pts)
# Render the sprint chart templates locally and save to rendered.yaml
# Then extract ONLY the Deployment kind from the rendered output
helm template sprint-dev ./sprint > rendered.yaml
grep -A 50 "kind: Deployment" rendered.yaml | head -30
T7
Package & Repo (4 min, 10 pts)
# Package the sprint chart, then create a local repo index
helm package ./sprint
# Creates sprint-0.1.0.tgz
mkdir -p local-repo
mv sprint-0.1.0.tgz local-repo/
helm repo index local-repo/
helm repo add local file://$(pwd)/local-repo
helm repo update
helm search repo local/
T8
Release Inspection (3 min, 10 pts)
# Show the manifest, values, and history of sprint-prod
helm get manifest sprint-prod -n sprint-prod-ns | head -20
helm get values sprint-prod -n sprint-prod-ns --all | head -20
helm history sprint-prod -n sprint-prod-ns
T9
Dependency Addition (3 min, 10 pts)
# Add a dependency to sprint/Chart.yaml and update
# Dependency: common chart (or skip if no network)
cat >> sprint/Chart.yaml <
T10
Cleanup (2 min, 10 pts)
# Uninstall both releases and verify nothing remains
helm uninstall sprint-dev -n sprint-ns
helm uninstall sprint-prod -n sprint-prod-ns
helm list -A | grep sprint  # Should be empty
# Score: __/100
🎯
Scoring Rubric: 10 pts per task. 70+ = exam-ready. 85+ = strong. 95+ = guaranteed pass. Time yourself strictly. If you finish with >5 minutes remaining AND score 95+, you're in the top tier. Repeat this lab daily until you hit 95+ in under 25 minutes.
Q1
You created a chart with helm create myapp but the deployment uses nginx. How do you change it to deploy your custom app?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Edit values.yaml: change image.repository to your app and image.tag to your version. Edit templates/deployment.yaml: change container port, add env vars, update health check paths. The default nginx chart is a template — customize it for your app.

Explanation

helm create scaffolds a complete chart with Chart.yaml, values.yaml, templates/, and helpers. On the exam, always use this — never start from an empty directory. Customize the generated files. Saves 5-10 minutes per chart task. 

helm create myapp
# Creates:
myapp/
├── Chart.yaml          # Metadata (apiVersion, name, version)
├── values.yaml         # Default configuration values
├── charts/             # Dependency charts go here
├── templates/
│   ├── deployment.yaml
│   ├── service.yaml
│   ├── hpa.yaml
│   ├── ingress.yaml
│   ├── serviceaccount.yaml
│   ├── NOTES.txt       # Post-install message to users
│   ├── _helpers.tpl    # Named reusable template blocks
│   └── tests/
│       └── test-connection.yaml
└── .helmignore         # Files excluded from chart package

# Exam tip: helm create + customize = fastest path to a valid chart

Q2
After helm install, pods show CrashLoopBackOff. What's your debugging sequence?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

1. kubectl logs deploy/<name> -n <ns> — see application errors. 2. kubectl describe pod <name> — check events for image pull errors, OOM kills. 3. helm get values <release> --all — verify configuration. 4. Check if dependencies (DB, Redis) are running and reachable.

Explanation

helm install creates a new release tracked in Kubernetes Secrets. Key flags: --atomic (auto-rollback), --wait (wait for readiness), --dry-run (validate first). Always dry-run before deploying on the exam.

Q3
You need to add PostgreSQL and Redis as dependencies. What are the exact steps?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

1. Add to Chart.yaml: dependencies: [{name: postgresql, version: "12.x.x", repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami}, {name: redis, version: "~18.0.0", repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami}]. 2. Run helm dependency update. 3. Reference in templates via {{ .Release.Name }}-postgresql for service discovery.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Standard install command:
helm install RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE --create-namespace

# Install with values file:

# Install with --set overrides:
helm install RELEASE ./chart --set image.tag=v2.0 -n NAMESPACE

# Install with --atomic (auto-rollback on failure):
helm install RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE --atomic --wait --timeout 5m
Q4
How do you create a database migration hook that runs before every upgrade?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Create a Job template with annotations: "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade, "helm.sh/hook-weight": "5", "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded. The Job runs python manage.py migrate --noinput using the same image. Deploy with helm upgrade --install — the hook runs automatically.

Explanation

Hooks run at lifecycle events via "helm.sh/hook" annotation. Types: pre/post-install/upgrade/delete/rollback, test. Synchronous — block the release. Use weights for ordering and delete policies for cleanup.

Q5
Your chart has a ConfigMap template. How do you verify it renders correctly before deploying?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

1. helm lint ./chart --strict — syntax check. 2. helm template test ./chart -f values.yaml --debug — local render. 3. Check output: grep for ConfigMap, verify values are substituted correctly. 4. helm install test ./chart --dry-run --debug — cluster validation.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

Q6
What command packages a chart for distribution and where does the output go?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

helm package ./chart creates a chartname-version.tgz file in the current directory. Push to OCI: helm push chart-0.1.0.tgz oci://registry.example.com/charts. The .tgz contains all chart files except those in .helmignore.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Creates: anihpj-chart-0.1.0.tgz

Q7
You deployed an app but forgot to enable ingress. The chart has an ingress template controlled by ingress.enabled. How do you fix this?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

helm upgrade <release> ./chart --set ingress.enabled=true -n <ns> --atomic --wait. The conditional template {{ if .Values.ingress.enabled }} will now render the Ingress resource. No need to reinstall — upgrade adds the missing resource.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Upgrade with auto-rollback:

Q8
During Lab 5's simulation, you upgrade to replicaCount=5 but the pods don't scale. What's likely wrong?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Check: 1. helm get values <release> --all | grep replicaCount — did the value actually change? 2. kubectl get deploy <name> -o yaml | grep replicas — is the deployment updated? 3. Resource quota might be limiting pod count. 4. HPA might be overriding replicas if autoscaling is enabled.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Release storage (per revision):

# sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v1
# sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v2
# sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v3

# Each Secret contains:
# - Chart metadata (name, version)
# - Computed values (all overrides merged)
# - Rendered manifests (the actual YAML applied)
# - Release info (status, timestamps)

# Inspect a revision:
kubectl get secret sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v2 -n prod -o jsonpath='{.data.release}' | base64 -d | gzip -d | python -m json.tool
Q9
How do you test that a deployed chart is actually working correctly?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

1. helm test <release> -n <ns> --logs — runs test hook pods. 2. helm status <release> --show-resources — check all resources healthy. 3. kubectl port-forward svc/<name> 8080:<port> then curl localhost:8080/health/. 4. Check pod logs for startup errors.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Hook annotations on a Job resource:
metadata:
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade          # Hook type
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "-5"          # Execution order
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded

# Available hook types:
# pre-install, post-install, pre-upgrade, post-upgrade,
# pre-delete, post-delete, pre-rollback, post-rollback, test

# Weights: Lower numbers execute FIRST
# Deletion policies: hook-succeeded, hook-failed, before-hook-creation

17.2 Chart Structure & Templates (20 Questions)
