Q1
What command scaffolds a new chart?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

helm create <chart-name>. Creates Chart.yaml, values.yaml, templates/, and helpers.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Minimal valid Chart.yaml:
apiVersion: v2
name: mychart
version: 0.1.0
type: application

# Full Chart.yaml reference:
apiVersion: v2
name: anihpj
version: 0.2.0
appVersion: "2.1.0"
description: A Helm chart for the anihpj job board application
type: application
kubeVersion: ">=1.25.0-0"
maintainers:
  - name: DevOps Team
    email: devops@example.com
icon: https://example.com/anihpj-icon.svg
keywords:
  - django
  - job-board
  - python
Q2
What are the five Built-in Objects available in templates?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

.Values, .Release, .Chart, .Files, .Capabilities (plus .Template).

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# template vs include - Key Difference:

# template: writes directly to output (NO piping)
{{ template "mylib.labels" . }}

# include: returns a string (CAN pipe through functions)
{{ include "mylib.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
{{ include "mylib.labels" . | quote }}

# Named template definition:
{{- define "anihpj.labels" -}}
app.kubernetes.io/name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }}
{{- end }}

# Usage:
metadata:
  labels:
    {{- include "anihpj.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
Q3
How do you conditionally include a resource?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

{{ if .Values.ingress.enabled }}...{{ end }}. The entire resource block is wrapped in the conditional.

Explanation

The five built-in objects are: .Values (config), .Release (release metadata), .Chart (chart metadata), .Files (static file access), .Capabilities (cluster info). Plus .Template for template info.

Q4
What's the difference between template and include?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

template writes inline (no pipeline). include returns a string (supports | indent, | quote). Always prefer include.

Explanation

Helm uses if for conditionals: {{ if .Values.ingress.enabled }}...{{ end }}. Wrap entire resources. Use eq, ne, lt, gt, and, or, not for comparisons. Resource-level conditionals are standard practice.

Q5
How do you embed a file from the chart into a ConfigMap?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

{{ .Files.Get "config/nginx.conf" | indent 4 }}. Files outside templates/ are accessible via .Files.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# template vs include - Key Difference:

# template: writes directly to output (NO piping)
{{ template "mylib.labels" . }}

# include: returns a string (CAN pipe through functions)
{{ include "mylib.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
{{ include "mylib.labels" . | quote }}

# Named template definition:
{{- define "anihpj.labels" -}}
app.kubernetes.io/name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }}
{{- end }}

# Usage:
metadata:
  labels:
    {{- include "anihpj.labels" . | nindent 4 }}

17.3 Values & Configuration (15 Questions)

17.7 Production Readiness Questions

P1
Your chart deploys successfully in dev but fails in production with Error: UPGRADE FAILED: rendered manifests contain a resource that already exists. What's the most likely cause and fix?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

The production namespace likely has pre-existing resources with the same names. Check what's already there with kubectl get all -n production. Either: (1) delete conflicting resources, (2) use a different release name, or (3) set fullnameOverride to avoid naming conflicts.

Explanation

Helm uses the release name + chart name to generate resource names via the fullname template in _helpers.tpl. If someone manually created resources or another release used the same naming pattern, conflicts occur. fullnameOverride in values.yaml lets you explicitly set the resource name prefix.

P2
You need to deploy the same chart 5 times in the same namespace with different configurations. What's the best practice?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Use different release names with different values files. Each release name creates a separate Helm release with its own resources, history, and lifecycle.

helm install anihpj-api ./chart -f values-api.yaml -n services
helm install anihpj-worker ./chart -f values-worker.yaml -n services
helm install anihpj-scheduler ./chart -f values-scheduler.yaml -n services
# All in the same namespace, all from the same chart,
# but independent releases with different configs
Explanation

This is the microservice deployment pattern. One chart, many releases. Each release gets its own Secret for history storage (sh.helm.release.v1.RELEASE-NAME.vN). They can be upgraded, rolled back, and uninstalled independently — even in the same namespace.

P3
helm list -n prod shows a release in pending-upgrade state for 10 minutes. What happened and how do you fix it?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

The previous helm upgrade command was interrupted (Ctrl+C, network timeout, or terminal closed) before completing. Helm left a pending-upgrade Secret that blocks further operations. Find and delete it:

kubectl get secrets -n prod -l owner=helm,status=pending-upgrade
kubectl delete secret -n prod -l owner=helm,status=pending-upgrade
helm rollback RELEASE -n prod  # Return to last good state
Explanation

When Helm starts an operation, it creates a "pending" Secret to lock the release. If the operation is interrupted, the lock persists. Deleting the pending Secret removes the lock, but the release may be in an inconsistent state — always rollback to be safe.

P4
How do you identify which Kubernetes resources were created by which Helm release?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Helm automatically adds labels to all deployed resources. You can filter by these labels:

# Find all resources from a specific release:
kubectl get all -n prod -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=myapp

# Find all Helm-managed resources:
kubectl get all -A -l app.kubernetes.io/managed-by=Helm

# Find resources from a specific chart:
kubectl get all -A -l helm.sh/chart=anihpj-0.1.0
Explanation

The standard labels (from _helpers.tpl) include: app.kubernetes.io/instance (release name), app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: Helm, helm.sh/chart (chart name + version). These are the "fingerprint" Helm leaves on every resource it manages. Use them to audit, filter, and debug.

P5
Your organization requires all deployments to have specific security labels. Where should you add them — in each template file or somewhere centralized?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Add them to _helpers.tpl as a named template that ALL resource templates include. This way, changing the labels in one place updates all resources.

{{- define "anihpj.securityLabels" -}}
security.company.com/data-classification: {{ .Values.security.dataClass }}
security.company.com/compliance: sox-pci
security.company.com/team: {{ .Values.security.team | default "platform" }}
{{- end }}
# Then in every template:
metadata:
  labels:
    {{- include "anihpj.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
    {{- include "anihpj.securityLabels" . | nindent 4 }}
Explanation

Centralizing labels in _helpers.tpl is the DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) pattern for Helm. This also makes it easy to add a Library Chart with standard labels that all your organization's charts can import.

class="cka-exam-questions">
Q1
What is the value precedence order?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

--set (highest) → -f files (last wins) → parent chart values → values.yaml → subchart defaults (lowest).

Explanation

Value precedence (highest to lowest): --set → -f files (last wins) → parent chart values → values.yaml → subchart defaults. --set always beats everything else.

Q2
How do you override a value during install?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

helm install app ./chart --set image.tag=v3.0. For nested: --set service.port=8080.

Explanation

Value precedence (highest to lowest): --set → -f files (last wins) → parent chart values → values.yaml → subchart defaults. --set always beats everything else.

Q3
What file provides JSON Schema validation for values?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

values.schema.json. Helm auto-validates user values against this schema at install/upgrade time.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Standard install command:
helm install RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE --create-namespace

# Install with values file:
helm install RELEASE ./chart -f values.yaml -n NAMESPACE

# Install with --set overrides:
helm install RELEASE ./chart --set image.tag=v2.0 -n NAMESPACE

# Install with --atomic (auto-rollback on failure):
helm install RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE --atomic --wait --timeout 5m

17.4 Advanced Features (15 Questions)

17.6 Scenario-Based Challenge Questions

These multi-step scenarios test your ability to combine multiple Helm concepts — just like the real exam.

17.8 95%+ Challenge Questions — Multi-Concept Scenarios

These questions combine 2-3 Helm concepts — exactly like the hardest exam questions. If you can answer these correctly, you're ready for 95%+.

H1
Scenario: You helm install app ./chart -n prod --set image.tag=v1.0. A colleague runs helm upgrade app ./chart -n prod --reuse-values without any flags. What image tag is now deployed?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

v1.0. --reuse-values preserves ALL previously set values, including the --set image.tag=v1.0 from the original install. Even though no --set was used in the upgrade, the old --set value is remembered and reused.

Explanation

This is the #1 gotcha with --reuse-values. Helm remembers ALL values from the previous release — including --set values, -f file values, AND chart defaults merged together. Using --reuse-values means "keep everything exactly as it was, only change what I explicitly override now." If you use --reuse-values and DON'T override the image tag, it stays at v1.0 even if the chart's values.yaml now says v2.0.

# TRACE THE VALUES:
# Initial install: helm install app ./chart --set image.tag=v1.0 -n prod
#   Computed values: {replicaCount: 1 (default), image.tag: v1.0 (--set)}
# 
# Upgrade with --reuse-values:
#   helm upgrade app ./chart -n prod --reuse-values
#   Computed values: {replicaCount: 1 (reused), image.tag: v1.0 (REUSED!)}
#   Chart's values.yaml says v2.0 but --reuse-values ignores it!
# 
# Upgrade WITHOUT --reuse-values (also no --reset-values):
#   helm upgrade app ./chart -n prod
#   Computed values: {replicaCount: 1 (chart default), image.tag: v1.0 (REMEMBERED!)}
#   Even without --reuse-values, previous --set values are remembered!
#   This is the "sticky --set" behavior.
# 
# Upgrade with --reset-values:
#   helm upgrade app ./chart -n prod --reset-values
#   Computed values: {replicaCount: 1 (chart default), image.tag: v2.0 (chart default)}
#   ONLY --reset-values truly discards previous --set values.
H2
Scenario: Your chart has a template: {{ .Values.db.password | b64enc }}. The value in values.yaml is db.password: changeme. You install with --set db.password=secret123. What is the base64-encoded value in the Secret?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

c2VjcmV0MTIz — the base64 encoding of "secret123". Because --set has the highest precedence, it overrides values.yaml's changeme. The template receives secret123, and b64enc encodes that.

Explanation

This tests value precedence AND template function understanding simultaneously. --set is priority #1, so the template sees "secret123" not "changeme". b64enc encodes whatever string it receives. The Secret's data field will contain the base64 of "secret123".

# Value precedence in action:
# values.yaml:     db.password = "changeme"    (priority 5, lowest)
# --set:           db.password = "secret123"   (priority 1, highest)
# Template sees:   "secret123"
# b64enc output:   c2VjcmV0MTIz

# Verify:
echo -n "secret123" | base64
# c2VjcmV0MTIz
H3
Scenario: Your Deployment template uses {{ include "mylib.labels" . | nindent 4 }} inside a range .Values.env block. The template fails with "nil pointer." Why?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Inside range, the dot (.) is rebound to the current loop element. So . no longer refers to the root context. include "mylib.labels" . passes the loop element (an env var) instead of the root, causing the nil pointer.

Explanation

This is the classic "dot rebinding" trap. Inside range and with, . changes. You must save the root context before entering a scope-changing block. ALWAYS use {{- $ := . -}} at the top of templates that use range/with.

# WRONG — dot is rebound inside range:
{{ range .Values.env }}
  labels:
    {{ include "mylib.labels" . | nindent 4 }}  ← . is now an env item!
  - name: {{ .name }}
{{ end }}

# RIGHT — save root context first:
{{- $root := . -}}
{{ range .Values.env }}
  labels:
    {{ include "mylib.labels" $root | nindent 4 }}  ← $root is the original .
  - name: {{ .name }}  ← . here is the env item (correct)
{{ end }}
H4
Scenario: You run helm upgrade app ./chart --atomic --timeout 2m. The pre-upgrade hook takes 90 seconds, the post-upgrade hook takes 60 seconds, and pods take 30 seconds to become ready. Does the upgrade succeed?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

NO — it times out. Total time: 90s (pre-hook) + 60s (post-hook) + 30s (pods) = 180 seconds. But --timeout 2m = 120 seconds. The upgrade fails and --atomic triggers auto-rollback.

Explanation

The --timeout is a TOTAL timeout for the ENTIRE operation — hooks + resource creation + waiting for readiness. If hooks consume most of the time budget, there's none left for the actual deployment. Always calculate: hook time + pod startup time + buffer = minimum timeout.

# TIMEOUT CALCULATION:
# Pre-install hooks:  0s (none) or variable
# Pre-upgrade hooks:  90s
# Resource creation:  5s
# Pod startup:       30s
# Post-install hooks: 60s
# ─────────────────────────
# TOTAL NEEDED:      185s
# 
# SAFE TIMEOUT: --timeout 5m (300s = 185s + 115s buffer)
# AGGRESSIVE:  --timeout 4m (240s = just enough)
# FAIL:         --timeout 2m (120s < 185s needed)
H5
Scenario: Your chart is at version 0.1.0. You make a breaking change to the template structure (renamed several value keys). What version should the chart be, and how do you communicate this to users?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Bump to 0.2.0 (MINOR version increment for breaking changes pre-1.0.0). Document ALL renamed keys in the CHANGELOG and NOTES.txt. After 1.0.0, breaking changes require a MAJOR version bump (1.0.0 → 2.0.0).

# SemVer for charts:
# MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH
# 
# Pre-1.0.0 (0.x.y):
#   PATCH (0.1.0→0.1.1): Bug fixes, no behavior change
#   MINOR (0.1.0→0.2.0): Breaking changes allowed
# 
# Post-1.0.0:
#   PATCH (1.0.0→1.0.1): Bug fixes, backwards-compatible
#   MINOR (1.0.0→1.1.0): New features, backwards-compatible
#   MAJOR (1.0.0→2.0.0): Breaking changes
# 
# DEPRECATION PATTERN:
# 1. v1.0.0: Add new key, deprecate old key (NOTES.txt warning)
# 2. v1.1.0: Old key still works but loud warnings
# 3. v2.0.0: Remove old key entirely (MAJOR bump)
class="cka-exam-questions">
S1
Scenario: You need to deploy WordPress with MariaDB in production. WordPress must connect to MariaDB, and both must be in the same namespace. MariaDB's root password should NEVER be in values.yaml. How do you set this up?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

1. Add MariaDB as a dependency in Chart.yaml with a condition. 2. Use --set or a sealed secret for the MariaDB password. 3. Import MariaDB's credentials into WordPress values via import-values. 4. Use helm install wordpress ./chart --set mariadb.auth.rootPassword=$(generate-password).

Explanation

This tests three concepts simultaneously: subchart dependencies, secrets management, and value importing. The key insight is that you should never hardcode passwords — always inject them at deploy time or use an external secrets manager.

S2
Scenario: A release anihpj-prod revision 17 is broken. Revision 15 was known good. However, someone manually deleted 3 releases' Secrets. helm rollback fails. What do you do?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

1. Check which revisions still exist: helm history anihpj-prod. 2. If revision 15's Secret is deleted, you cannot rollback to it. 3. Instead, retrieve a known-good values file and redeploy: helm upgrade anihpj-prod ./chart -f values-good.yaml --reset-values. 4. Implement a backup strategy for release Secrets going forward.

Explanation

Helm stores each revision as a Secret. If the Secret is deleted, that revision is permanently lost. This is why production environments should back up Helm release Secrets or use an external SQL storage backend. --reset-values is critical here — it discards all previous --set values and uses only what's in the values file.

S3
Scenario: Your chart's Deployment template renders differently on K8s 1.24 vs 1.28 because the API version changed. How do you make the chart compatible with both?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Use .Capabilities.APIVersions.Has or semverCompare on .Capabilities.KubeVersion to conditionally select the correct API version in the template.

{{ if .Capabilities.APIVersions.Has "apps/v1" }}
apiVersion: apps/v1
{{ else }}
apiVersion: apps/v1beta2
{{ end }}
kind: Deployment
Explanation

The .Capabilities object is Helm's way of detecting what the target cluster supports. Always use it when a resource API version is deprecated across K8s versions. This is especially relevant for Ingress (networking.k8s.io/v1 vs v1beta1), PodSecurityPolicy (removed in 1.25), and CronJob (batch/v1 vs batch/v1beta1).

S4
Scenario: You run helm upgrade anihpj ./chart --atomic --timeout 3m. The upgrade starts, a pre-upgrade hook runs for 2 minutes, then the new pods start but one stays in Pending for 3 more minutes. What happens?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

The upgrade will time out after 3 minutes total and automatically rollback (because of --atomic). The hook's 2 minutes counts toward the timeout! The pending pod never gets a chance to start. Helm marks the release as failed and reverts to the previous revision.

Explanation

--timeout is a TOTAL timeout for the entire operation, including hooks. If hooks take 2 minutes and pods need 3 minutes to start, you need at least --timeout 6m. Always set generous timeouts in production — the default 5 minutes is often insufficient for complex deployments with hooks and large images.

S5
Scenario: Your team wants to share common label templates, security context definitions, and naming conventions across 5 different microservice charts. Each chart should import these shared definitions without duplicating code. What Helm feature enables this?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Library Charts (type: library in Chart.yaml). Create a library chart with {{ define "..." }} blocks for common patterns. Each microservice chart adds the library as a dependency and uses {{ include "..." . }} to invoke the shared templates.

Explanation

Library charts are the Helm equivalent of shared code libraries. They contain only templates/ (no deployable resources) and expose named templates via define. This is the DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) pattern for Helm at organizational scale. Change one library template, and all consuming charts benefit on next upgrade.

17.9 Rapid-Fire Knowledge Check — 60-Second Questions

These test your instant recall. You should answer each in under 60 seconds. If you can't, review the referenced chapter.

R1
What flag makes helm install wait for all pods to be ready?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

--wait

Explanation

--wait blocks until all Pods, PVCs, Services, and minimum replicas of Deployments/StatefulSets are in a ready state. Combine with --timeout to set a maximum wait time.

R2
What's the difference between template and include?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

template writes directly to output (no piping). include returns a string (can pipe through functions like nindent, quote).

Explanation

Always use include for named templates in resource definitions. Only use template for standalone output where you don't need to transform the result.

R3
Where does Helm 3 store release history?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Kubernetes Secrets named sh.helm.release.v1.<name>.v<rev>

Explanation

Default storage backend. Each revision gets a separate Secret in the release namespace. Label for filtering: owner=helm. Max 1MB per Secret — use SQL backend for larger manifests.

R4
What flag auto-rolls back on upgrade failure?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

--atomic (Helm 3) / --rollback-on-failure (Helm 4)

Explanation

If the upgrade fails, --atomic automatically rolls back to the last successful revision. Combine with --cleanup-on-fail to remove failed resources.

R5
What annotation makes a resource a Helm hook?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

"helm.sh/hook": <type> where type is pre-install, post-install, pre-upgrade, etc.

Explanation

Hook types: pre/post-install, pre/post-upgrade, pre/post-delete, pre/post-rollback, test. Combined with weight and delete-policy annotations to control execution.

R6
How do you list releases across all namespaces?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

helm list -A or helm list --all-namespaces

Explanation

helm list -A --failed shows only failed releases. helm list -n NS scopes to a specific namespace.

R7
What's the Helm command to see rendered templates without installing?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

helm template NAME ./chart

Explanation

Renders templates locally without connecting to Kubernetes. Use --debug for detailed output. Different from --dry-run which DOES connect to the K8s API for validation.

R8
How do you add a chart repository?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

helm repo add NAME URL then helm repo update

Explanation

Repositories are stored in repositories.yaml. Always run helm repo update after adding to fetch the index. Use helm repo list to see configured repos.

R9
What function prevents nil pointer errors in templates?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

default — e.g., {{ .Values.opt | default "fallback" }}

Explanation

default returns the fallback if the value is nil, empty string, false, zero, or empty collection. required does the opposite — it throws an error if the value is empty.

R10
What flag installs a chart if it doesn't exist, and upgrades if it does?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

--install on helm upgrade: helm upgrade --install NAME ./chart

Explanation

This is the idempotent deploy pattern. Safe for CI/CD — works whether it's the first deploy or the hundredth. Combine with --atomic --wait --create-namespace for production.

class="cka-exam-questions">
Q1
Where are chart dependencies declared?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

In Chart.yaml under the dependencies: key. Each specifies name, version constraint, and repository.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Standard install command:
helm install RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE --create-namespace

# Install with values file:
helm install RELEASE ./chart -f values.yaml -n NAMESPACE

# Install with --set overrides:
helm install RELEASE ./chart --set image.tag=v2.0 -n NAMESPACE

# Install with --atomic (auto-rollback on failure):
helm install RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE --atomic --wait --timeout 5m
Q2
What annotation marks a resource as a Helm hook?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

"helm.sh/hook": <type> (e.g., pre-install, post-upgrade). Jobs are the most common hook resource.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Hook annotations on a Job resource:
metadata:
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade          # Hook type
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "-5"          # Execution order
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded

# Available hook types:
# pre-install, post-install, pre-upgrade, post-upgrade,
# pre-delete, post-delete, pre-rollback, post-rollback, test

# Weights: Lower numbers execute FIRST
# Deletion policies: hook-succeeded, hook-failed, before-hook-creation
Q3
How do you run chart tests?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

helm test <release>. Executes test hook resources. Use --logs to see output.

Explanation

Hooks run at lifecycle events via "helm.sh/hook" annotation. Types: pre/post-install/upgrade/delete/rollback, test. Synchronous — block the release. Use weights for ordering and delete policies for cleanup.

17.5 CI/CD & Production (10 Questions)

Q1
What is the idempotent install/upgrade command for CI/CD?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

helm upgrade --install <release> ./chart -f values.yaml -n <ns> --atomic --wait --timeout 10m.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Standard upgrade:
helm upgrade RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE

# Upgrade with new values:
helm upgrade RELEASE ./chart -f values-new.yaml -n NAMESPACE

# Upgrade-or-install (idempotent):
helm upgrade --install RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE

# Upgrade with auto-rollback:
helm upgrade RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE --atomic --cleanup-on-fail
Q2
How should secrets be managed in CI/CD pipelines using Helm?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Inject via CI/CD variables: --set dbPassword=$CI_SECRET. Never store secrets in values.yaml committed to Git.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# values.yaml with documented defaults:
replicaCount: 3
image:
  repository: anihpj        # Docker image repository
  tag: v2.0.0                # Image tag (pin in production!)
  pullPolicy: IfNotPresent   # Image pull policy

service:
  type: ClusterIP            # ClusterIP | NodePort | LoadBalancer
  port: 80                   # Service port

ingress:
  enabled: true              # Enable/disable Ingress resource
  className: nginx           # Ingress class name
  host: anihpj.example.com   # Ingress hostname
  tls: true                  # Enable TLS

# Access in templates: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
# Override: --set replicaCount=5
Q3
What is Helmfile used for?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Declarative management of multiple Helm releases. Define all releases in one YAML file, apply with helmfile apply.

Explanation

Never store plaintext secrets in values.yaml. Use placeholders, inject at deploy time (--set or CI/CD), encode with b64enc in templates. Production: Sealed Secrets, External Secrets Operator, or Vault.

Chapter 18: Helm Operations at Scale — Running Helm in Production

Running one or two releases is easy. Running 50+ releases across multiple clusters, managing release storage, monitoring for drift, and recovering from disasters — that's operations at scale. This chapter covers performance optimization, storage backends, SDK usage, monitoring, disaster recovery, and multi-cluster Helm strategies.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~2 hours 🏭 Operations 📈 Scale

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Optimize Helm performance for large charts and many releases
  • ✅ Understand release storage backends — Secrets vs ConfigMaps vs SQL
  • ✅ Use the Helm SDK for programmatic chart management
  • ✅ Monitor Helm releases for drift and health
  • ✅ Build disaster recovery plans — backup and restore release state
  • ✅ Manage Helm across multiple Kubernetes clusters

18.1 Helm Performance — Large Charts & Many Releases

As your Helm usage grows, performance becomes critical. A chart with 100+ templates, or managing 200+ releases, requires optimization strategies.

📊
Chart Size Optimization

Problem: Charts with 100+ templates take seconds to render. Solutions: Use library charts for shared templates, split monolithic charts into subcharts, use .helmignore to exclude unnecessary files from packaging, keep templates focused — one resource per template file.

🚀
Release Count Optimization

Problem: helm list slows down with 200+ releases. Solutions: Use --namespace scoping, increase --history-max carefully (each revision stores a full Secret), clean up old failed releases, consider using --keep-history sparingly.

⚡
Template Caching

Helm caches downloaded charts in ~/.cache/helm/. For CI/CD, warm the cache in your pipeline image or use helm dependency build with a pre-populated charts/ directory to skip downloads.

🔧
API Rate Limiting

Large-scale installs can hit K8s API rate limits. Use --wait judiciously (it polls the API), batch releases with Helmfile's --concurrency, and consider increasing K8s API server QPS if you control the cluster.

Performance Commands
# See how many releases and revisions exist
helm list -A | wc -l
kubectl get secrets -A -l owner=helm | wc -l

# Clean up old failed releases
helm list -A --failed | awk 'NR>1{print $1}' | while read r; do
  helm uninstall "$r" -n $(helm list -A | grep "$r" | awk '{print $2}')
done

# Limit release history
helm install myapp ./chart --history-max 5
helm upgrade myapp ./chart --history-max 5

18.2 Release Storage Backends — Secrets vs ConfigMaps vs SQL

Helm 3 stores release history as Kubernetes Secrets by default. But for enterprise-scale deployments, alternative backends offer better performance and manageability.

BackendDefault inProsCons
SecretsHelm 3Encrypted at rest (some K8s distros), native RBAC, no extra infra1MB size limit per Secret, large manifests may exceed it
ConfigMapsHelm 2 (legacy)Simple, easy to inspectPlain text, less secure, same 1MB limit. Not recommended.
SQL (PostgreSQL)Helm 3.3+ via SDKNo size limit, fast queries, backup-friendly, proper indexingExtra infrastructure, requires Helm SDK integration
📖 SQL Storage Driver

Introduced in Helm 3.3+, the SQL storage driver stores releases in PostgreSQL. Benefits: no 1MB Secret limit, efficient release listing with SQL queries, easier backup/recovery. Requires helm.sh/storage-driver: sql configuration. Primarily used via the Helm SDK for programmatic access — not yet a first-class CLI feature.

Storage Backend Decision Flow
  WHICH STORAGE BACKEND SHOULD YOU USE?

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  START: How many releases do you manage?                        │
  │                                                                  │
  │  < 50 releases? ──▶ Secrets (Default)                          │
  │  ✅ Simple, no extra infra, encrypted at rest.                  │
  │                                                                  │
  │  50-200 releases? ──▶ Secrets + strict history-max              │
  │  ✅ Still viable. Set --history-max 5. Clean up failed releases. │
  │                                                                  │
  │  200+ releases? ──▶ Consider SQL Driver                          │
  │  ✅ No 1MB limit. Efficient queries. Better backup.              │
  │                                                                  │
  │  Manifests > 1MB? ──▶ MUST use SQL Driver                      │
  │  ⚠️ Secrets have a hard 1MB limit. You CANNOT store large       │
  │     manifests in Secrets. Split chart OR use SQL.                │
  │                                                                  │
  │  🔑 For 99% of teams: Secrets are sufficient.                   │
  │     SQL Driver is for Helm-at-scale (platform teams, operators). │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

18.3 Helm SDK — Programmatic Chart Management

The Helm Go SDK lets you embed Helm operations directly into your Go applications — install, upgrade, rollback charts programmatically. Used by tools like Argo CD, Flux, and custom operators.

Helm SDK — Go Example (Conceptual)
import (
    "helm.sh/helm/v3/pkg/action"
    "helm.sh/helm/v3/pkg/chart/loader"
    "helm.sh/helm/v3/pkg/cli"
)

func installChart(name, namespace, chartPath string) error {
    settings := cli.New()
    actionConfig := new(action.Configuration)
    actionConfig.Init(settings.RESTClientGetter(), namespace, "secrets", nil)

    chart, _ := loader.Load(chartPath)
    install := action.NewInstall(actionConfig)
    install.ReleaseName = name
    install.Namespace = namespace
    install.Atomic = true
    install.Wait = true

    _, err := install.Run(chart, map[string]interface{}{})
    return err
}
🔧
Who Uses the SDK?

Argo CD — renders Helm charts for GitOps, Flux CD — Helm controller, Terraform Helm Provider — manages releases via Terraform, Custom Operators — Kubernetes operators that deploy apps via Helm.

💡
Why Use the SDK?

When you need programmatic control: dynamic value injection, custom release naming logic, integration with internal systems, or embedding Helm in a larger platform. Not for day-to-day CLI usage — for building tools that USE Helm.

💡 SDK vs CLI — When to Use Which

CLI = 99% of daily work. SDK = building tools (operators, GitOps controllers, deployment platforms). For the certification, understand the SDK conceptually — what it enables, not its Go API. The exam tests CLI proficiency, not Go programming.

18.4 Monitoring Helm Releases

Once deployed, you need to know if releases are healthy, if drift has occurred, and if any releases are in a failed state.

Helm Release Monitoring Strategy
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  HELM RELEASE MONITORING — THREE LAYERS                            │
  │                                                                     │
  │  LAYER 1: Release Health (Helm-level)                              │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────                              │
  │  helm list -A --failed          ← Find broken releases            │
  │  helm list -A --pending          ← Find stuck operations           │
  │  helm status <release> -n <ns>  ← Check individual health        │
  │                                                                     │
  │  LAYER 2: Resource Health (Kubernetes-level)                       │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────────────────                     │
  │  kubectl get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=<release>          │
  │  kubectl rollout status deploy/<name> -n <ns>                     │
  │                                                                     │
  │  LAYER 3: Application Health (App-level)                           │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────                          │
  │  helm test <release> -n <ns>     ← Run test hooks                 │
  │  Prometheus metrics / Grafana dashboards                            │
  │  Liveness/readiness probe monitoring                                │
  │                                                                     │
  │  🚨 DRIFT DETECTION:                                               │
  │  helm get manifest <release> | kubectl diff -f -                   │
  │  (or use helm-diff plugin: helm diff upgrade <release> ./chart)    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Health Check Commands
# Find all failed releases across the cluster
helm list -A --failed

# Check status with resource details
helm status anihpj-prod -n production --show-resources

# Detect drift — compare live state to Helm's last known state
helm get manifest anihpj-prod -n production | kubectl diff -f -

# Better drift detection with helm-diff plugin
helm plugin install https://github.com/databus/helm-diff
helm diff upgrade anihpj-prod ./anihpj-chart -f values-prod.yaml

18.5 Disaster Recovery — Backup & Restore Release State

Helm stores release state in Secrets. Backing them up is backing up your Helm release history. Without them, Helm doesn't know what it deployed.

1
Identify Release Secrets

kubectl get secrets -A -l owner=helm — These Secrets contain all release metadata, rendered manifests, and values. Each revision is a separate Secret named sh.helm.release.v1.<name>.v<rev>.

2
Backup Secrets

kubectl get secrets -A -l owner=helm -o yaml > helm-releases-backup.yaml. This saves ALL release history. For production, use Velero or etcd snapshots for comprehensive cluster backup that includes Helm Secrets.

3
Restore Secrets

kubectl apply -f helm-releases-backup.yaml — Re-creates the Secrets. After restore, Helm sees releases as "deployed" and can manage them normally. helm list should show all restored releases.

4
Verify Restoration

After restore: helm list -A, helm status <release>, helm get manifest <release>. If resources were also lost, run helm upgrade --install <release> ./chart -f values.yaml to recreate them.

⚠️ Backup Also: Chart Sources + Values Files + Repositories

Release Secrets contain rendered manifests — not chart source code. For complete DR: (1) Back up your chart Git repos, (2) Back up values files, (3) Back up release Secrets, (4) Document repository URLs and credentials. With all four, you can fully reconstruct any deployment from scratch.

DR Recovery Timeline — RPO & RTO for Helm Releases
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  HELM DR — RECOVERY POINT OBJECTIVE (RPO) & RECOVERY TIME (RTO)  │
  │                                                                   │
  │  SCENARIO                    RPO           RTO        TOOL       │
  │  ────────────────────────    ────────      ───────    ─────────  │
  │  Accidental uninstall        Last backup   ~5 min     helm install│
  │  (helm uninstall)            (if kept)                from backup │
  │                                                                    │
  │  Namespace deletion          Last etcd     ~10 min    kubectl     │
  │  (kubectl delete ns)         snapshot                 apply       │
  │                                                                    │
  │  Cluster-wide disaster       Last etcd     ~30 min    Velero or   │
  │  (control plane failure)     snapshot                 etcd restore│
  │                                                                    │
  │  Complete region loss        Last offsite ~2 hours   Velero with │
  │  (cloud region down)         backup                   S3 backup   │
  │                                                                    │
  │  🔑 GOLDEN RULE: Test your restore procedure quarterly.           │
  │     A backup you haven't tested is not a backup — it's a prayer.  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

18.6 Helm in Multi-Cluster Environments

Managing Helm across dev, staging, prod, and DR clusters requires a consistent strategy for kubeconfig management, release naming, and configuration.

Multi-Cluster Helm Strategy

  │  │ DEV CLUSTER │   │ STG CLUSTER │   │ PROD CLUSTER│             │
  │  │ (kubeconfig │   │ (kubeconfig │   │ (kubeconfig │             │
  │  │  dev.yaml)  │   │  stg.yaml)  │   │  prod.yaml) │             │
  │  └──────┬──────┘   └──────┬──────┘   └──────┬──────┘             │
  │         │                 │                 │                     │
  │         └─────────────────┼─────────────────┘                     │
  │                           │                                       │
  │                    ┌──────▼──────┐                                │
  │                    │  Helm CLI   │                                │
  │                    │ (switch via │                                │
  │                    │  KUBECONFIG │                                │
  │                    │  env var)   │                                │
  │                    └─────────────┘                                │
  │                                                                     │
  │  DEPLOY PATTERNS:                                                  │
  │  KUBECONFIG=dev.yaml  helm install dev  ./chart -f values-dev.yaml │
  │  KUBECONFIG=stg.yaml  helm install stg  ./chart -f values-stg.yaml │

🔀
Kubeconfig Switching

Use KUBECONFIG env var or kubectl config use-context to switch clusters. Helm uses the same kubeconfig as kubectl. Always verify: kubectl cluster-info BEFORE helm install.

📋
Helmfile for Multi-Cluster

Helmfile supports environments: with different kubeconfigs per environment. One helmfile.yaml can manage all clusters: helmfile -e prod apply.

🔄
Argo CD Multi-Cluster

Argo CD can deploy Helm charts to external clusters. Add external clusters to Argo CD, then specify destination.server in Application CRD. Argo handles kubeconfig and auth.

🏷️
Consistent Naming

Use a naming convention: <app>-<env> (e.g., anihpj-dev, anihpj-prod). This makes helm list -A readable across clusters. Combine with consistent namespace naming.

🎓 Multi-Cluster on the Exam

The exam typically uses a single cluster. However, you may be asked to switch contexts: kubectl config use-context <context-name>. Helm automatically follows the current kubectl context. Always verify: kubectl config current-context before deploying.

🏋️ Hands-On Drill: Scale Operations — Backup, Restore & Multi-Cluster Deploy

Scenario: You're the platform engineer for anihpj. You need to: (1) back up all releases, (2) simulate a disaster recovery, (3) deploy to a second cluster. Complete all tasks.

  1. Backup: Export ALL release secrets: kubectl get secrets -A -l owner=helm -o yaml > anihpj-helm-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d).yaml
  2. Audit: Count releases and revisions: helm list -A | wc -l and kubectl get secrets -A -l owner=helm | wc -l
  3. Simulate DR: helm uninstall anihpj-dev --keep-history then restore: kubectl apply -f anihpj-helm-backup.yaml
  4. Verify: helm list -A — should show anihpj-dev as "uninstalled" with history intact
  5. Find failed releases: helm list -A --failed — clean up any stale failures
  6. Switch context: kubectl config use-context staging-cluster then deploy: helm upgrade --install anihpj-stg ./chart -f values-staging.yaml -n staging --atomic --wait
  7. Verify multi-cluster: kubectl config get-contexts then check helm list -A on each cluster
✅ Complete Solution Script 
#!/bin/bash
set -e
echo "🔍 Auditing current state..."
helm list -A
echo "Releases: $(helm list -A | wc -l)"
echo "Secrets: $(kubectl get secrets -A -l owner=helm | wc -l)"

echo "💾 Backing up all releases..."
kubectl get secrets -A -l owner=helm -o yaml > helm-full-backup.yaml
echo "Backup size: $(du -h helm-full-backup.yaml | cut -f1)"

echo "🧹 Checking for failed releases..."
FAILED=$(helm list -A --failed -o json | jq -r '.[].name')
if [ -n "$FAILED" ]; then
  echo "Found failed releases: $FAILED"
  echo "Consider: helm uninstall  --keep-history"
fi

echo "🌐 Multi-cluster status:"
kubectl config get-contexts
echo "Current: $(kubectl config current-context)"
echo "✅ Operations audit complete!"

18.7 Release Storage Backends - Secrets vs ConfigMaps vs SQL

Helm 3 supports multiple storage backends for release information. The choice impacts performance, scalability, and disaster recovery capability.

BackendMax SizePerformanceBest ForRecovery
Secret (default)1 MBFast (etcd-native)Normal charts (<1MB rendered)kubectl backup
ConfigMap1 MBFast (etcd-native)Legacy (Helm 2 compat)kubectl backup
SQL (PostgreSQL, MySQL)UnlimitedModerate (DB query)Very large manifests (>1MB)DB backup/restore
Storage Backend Decision Flow
CHOOSING A STORAGE BACKEND:
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Is your rendered manifest < 1MB?
  ├── YES → Use Secrets (default). Nothing to configure.
  │         helm install NAME ./chart  (uses Secrets)
  │
  └── NO → Use SQL backend.
            Set HELM_DRIVER=sql
            Configure HELM_DRIVER_SQL_CONNECTION_STRING
            helm install NAME ./chart --storage-driver sql

SQL CONNECTION STRING FORMAT:
PostgreSQL: postgresql://user:pass@host:5432/helm?sslmode=disable
MySQL:      mysql://user:pass@tcp(host:3306)/helm

SETUP:
export HELM_DRIVER=sql
export HELM_DRIVER_SQL_CONNECTION_STRING="postgresql://helm:pass@db:5432/helm"
helm install NAME ./chart  # Auto-uses SQL

18.8 Helm Performance Optimization

⚡
Install/Upgrade Speed
  • --wait vs --no-hooks: --wait blocks until pods are ready. Skip for CI testing with --no-hooks
  • --timeout: Lower timeout means faster failure detection. Default 5m is often too long for CI
  • Parallel installs: Different namespaces can install in parallel safely
  • Chart size: Large templates/ directory slows rendering. Use .helmignore to exclude unnecessary files
📊
Release List Performance
  • helm list -A: Scans ALL namespaces. Slow with 1000+ releases. Use -n NS to scope
  • Release Secrets: Each revision is a Secret. Set --history-max 5 to limit storage
  • Label filtering: kubectl get secrets -l owner=helm,name=myapp is faster than helm list
  • SQL backend: Scales better than Secrets for 1000+ releases
class="cka-exam-questions">
Q1
What is the default storage backend for Helm 3 release history?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Kubernetes Secrets (in the release namespace). Helm 2 used ConfigMaps. Secrets are the default because they offer better security (encrypted at rest on many K8s distributions).

Explanation

Each release revision creates one Secret: sh.helm.release.v1.<name>.v<rev>. These Secrets contain the chart, values (including secrets!), and rendered manifests. The 1MB Secret size limit can be a problem for very large manifests — consider the SQL driver for those cases. 

# View release secrets:
kubectl get secrets -l owner=helm -n prod
# NAME                               TYPE     DATA
# sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v1     helm.sh/release.v1   1
# sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v2     helm.sh/release.v1   1

# Inspect revision:
kubectl get secret sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v2 -n prod -o jsonpath='{.data.release}' | base64 -d | gzip -d | jq .
# Output: {"name":"anihpj","chart":{...},"config":{...},"manifest":"---\napiVersion: apps/v1..."}

Explanation

default is the #1 safety function: {{ .Values.x | default "safe" }}. Prevents nil pointer panics — the most common Helm error. Every nullable value reference needs this.

Q2
How do you detect if someone manually modified resources deployed by Helm?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Use helm diff upgrade (helm-diff plugin) or helm get manifest <release> | kubectl diff -f -. This compares Helm's stored manifest with the live state in Kubernetes.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Standard install command:
helm install RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE --create-namespace

# Install with values file:
helm install RELEASE ./chart -f values.yaml -n NAMESPACE

# Install with --set overrides:
helm install RELEASE ./chart --set image.tag=v2.0 -n NAMESPACE

# Install with --atomic (auto-rollback on failure):
helm install RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE --atomic --wait --timeout 5m
Q3
What command backs up all Helm release Secrets?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

kubectl get secrets -A -l owner=helm -o yaml > helm-backup.yaml. The label owner=helm identifies all Helm release Secrets. Restore with kubectl apply -f helm-backup.yaml.

Explanation

Never store plaintext secrets in values.yaml. Use placeholders, inject at deploy time (--set or CI/CD), encode with b64enc in templates. Production: Sealed Secrets, External Secrets Operator, or Vault.

Q4
How do you manage Helm across multiple Kubernetes clusters?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Switch kubeconfig contexts: kubectl config use-context <cluster> or set KUBECONFIG=/path/to/config. Helm always uses the current kubectl context. For automation, use Helmfile with environment definitions or Argo CD for GitOps multi-cluster.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# values.yaml with documented defaults:
replicaCount: 3
image:
  repository: anihpj        # Docker image repository
  tag: v2.0.0                # Image tag (pin in production!)
  pullPolicy: IfNotPresent   # Image pull policy

service:
  type: ClusterIP            # ClusterIP | NodePort | LoadBalancer
  port: 80                   # Service port

ingress:
  enabled: true              # Enable/disable Ingress resource
  className: nginx           # Ingress class name
  host: anihpj.example.com   # Ingress hostname
  tls: true                  # Enable TLS

# Access in templates: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
# Override: --set replicaCount=5
Q5
What is the Helm SDK used for?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Programmatic Helm chart management from Go applications. Used by Argo CD, Flux, Terraform Helm Provider, and custom operators. The SDK provides Go APIs for install, upgrade, rollback, and uninstall operations.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Rollback to previous revision:
helm rollback RELEASE -n NAMESPACE

# Rollback to specific revision:
helm rollback RELEASE 3 -n NAMESPACE

# View history first:
helm history RELEASE -n NAMESPACE
# 1  Tue Jan 15 10:00:00 2024  SUPERSEDED  anihpj-0.1.0  1.0.0  Install complete
# 2  Tue Jan 15 10:30:00 2024  SUPERSEDED  anihpj-0.1.1  1.0.1  Upgrade complete
# 3  Tue Jan 15 11:00:00 2024  FAILED      anihpj-0.2.0  2.0.0  Upgrade failed

# Rollback creates a NEW revision:
helm rollback RELEASE 2 -n NAMESPACE
# Creates revision 4 with config from revision 2
Q6
What happens if a release Secret exceeds 1MB?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

The install/upgrade fails. Kubernetes Secrets have a 1MB hard limit. Solution: split monolithic charts into smaller subcharts, use the SQL storage driver, or reduce rendered manifest size by removing unnecessary resources.

Explanation

Never store plaintext secrets in values.yaml. Use placeholders, inject at deploy time (--set or CI/CD), encode with b64enc in templates. Production: Sealed Secrets, External Secrets Operator, or Vault.

Q7
How do you find all failed Helm releases across the cluster?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

helm list --all-namespaces --failed or helm list -A --failed. Also: --pending for stuck operations, --uninstalled with --all for uninstalled releases.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# List releases in current namespace:
helm list

# List ALL releases across ALL namespaces:
helm list -A

# List only failed releases:
helm list -A --failed

# List releases sorted by date:
helm list -A --date --reverse

# List with specific filter:
helm list -n production --filter anihpj
Q8
What performance issues arise with 200+ Helm releases?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

helm list becomes slow (queries all release Secrets). Solutions: namespace scoping, reducing history-max, cleaning up failed releases, using the SQL storage driver for better indexing.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# List releases in current namespace:
helm list

# List ALL releases across ALL namespaces:
helm list -A

# List only failed releases:
helm list -A --failed

# List releases sorted by date:
helm list -A --date --reverse

# List with specific filter:
helm list -n production --filter anihpj
Q9
What is the SQL storage driver and when should you use it?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Introduced in Helm 3.3+, stores releases in PostgreSQL instead of Secrets. Use when: (1) manifests exceed 1MB Secret limit, (2) you need efficient listing/queries at scale, (3) you want easier backup/recovery with SQL tools. Requires Helm SDK — not a CLI feature yet.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# SECRETS MANAGEMENT PATTERNS:

# NEVER do this:
# values.yaml:
#   password: mySecret123  ← COMMITTED TO GIT! DANGER!

# INSTEAD, use --set at deploy time:
helm install app ./chart --set db.password="$DB_PASS" -n prod

# Or use b64enc in templates:
data:
  password: {{ .Values.db.password | b64enc }}

# Or use Sealed Secrets / External Secrets Operator:
# These encrypt secrets so they can be committed to Git safely
Q10
What's the DR strategy for Helm releases?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

4-part backup: (1) Chart source code (Git), (2) Values files (Git), (3) Release Secrets (kubectl get secrets -A -l owner=helm), (4) Repository config (helm repo list). For comprehensive DR, use Velero or etcd snapshots to back up the entire cluster state.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# values.yaml with documented defaults:
replicaCount: 3
image:
  repository: anihpj        # Docker image repository
  tag: v2.0.0                # Image tag (pin in production!)
  pullPolicy: IfNotPresent   # Image pull policy

service:
  type: ClusterIP            # ClusterIP | NodePort | LoadBalancer
  port: 80                   # Service port

ingress:
  enabled: true              # Enable/disable Ingress resource
  className: nginx           # Ingress class name
  host: anihpj.example.com   # Ingress hostname
  tls: true                  # Enable TLS

# Access in templates: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
# Override: --set replicaCount=5

Chapter 19: Advanced Chart Patterns — Reusable, Scalable Helm

Beyond basic charts, Helm offers advanced patterns for maximum reusability. Library charts share template code across charts. Starter charts jump-start new projects. Feature toggles conditionally include resources. Post-renderers integrate Kustomize natively. These patterns separate intermediate users from Helm experts.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~2 hours 📐 Patterns 🏗️ Architecture

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Create reusable Library Charts for shared template code
  • ✅ Build Starter Charts for rapid project scaffolding
  • ✅ Design environment-specific chart patterns
  • ✅ Use Feature Toggles for conditional resource inclusion
  • ✅ Integrate Kustomize with Helm via Post-Renderers
  • ✅ Generate chart boilerplate automatically

19.1 Library Charts — Reusable Chart Components

A Library Chart (type: library) is NOT deployable — it only contains named templates that other charts import. Think of it as a "template-only" chart for shared helper functions and resource patterns.

Library Charts — How They Work
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  LIBRARY CHART PATTERN                                             │
  │                                                                     │
  │  ┌──────────────────────┐                                          │
  │  │ my-library/          │  ← type: library (NOT deployable)       │
  │  │ Chart.yaml           │                                          │
  │  │ templates/           │                                          │
  │  │   _labels.tpl        │  ← Shared label helpers                  │
  │  │   _deployment.tpl    │  ← Standard deployment template          │
  │  │   _service.tpl       │  ← Standard service template             │
  │  └────────┬─────────────┘                                          │
  │           │                                                        │
  │           │ imported by                                            │
  │           ▼                                                        │
  │  ┌──────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────┐             │
  │  │ myapp-chart/        │   │ otherapp-chart/      │             │
  │  │ Chart.yaml          │   │ Chart.yaml           │             │
  │  │ dependencies:       │   │ dependencies:        │             │
  │  │ - name: my-library  │   │ - name: my-library   │             │
  │  │   version: 1.0.0    │   │   version: 1.0.0     │             │
  │  │   repository: ...   │   │   repository: ...    │             │
  │  └──────────────────────┘   └──────────────────────┘             │
  │                                                                     │
  │  Both charts use {{ include "my-library.labels" . }}              │
  │  DRY principle: define template logic ONCE, use everywhere.        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Library Chart Example
# my-library/Chart.yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: my-library
type: library         # ← KEY: type must be "library"
version: 1.0.0

# my-library/templates/_standard-labels.tpl
{{- define "my-library.labels" -}}
app.kubernetes.io/name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
app.kubernetes.io/version: {{ .Chart.AppVersion }}
helm.sh/chart: {{ .Chart.Name }}-{{ .Chart.Version }}
app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: {{ .Release.Service }}
{{- end }}

# Usage in any chart that depends on my-library:
labels: {{ include "my-library.labels" . | nindent 4 }}

19.2 Starter Charts — helm create --starter

Starter charts are templates for helm create. Instead of the default nginx chart, you can scaffold from your organization's standardized chart template.

Starter Chart Workflow
# Create a starter chart
mkdir -p ~/.helm/starters/myorg-starter/templates
cat > ~/.helm/starters/myorg-starter/Chart.yaml <<EOF
apiVersion: v2
name: "{{ .Name }}"
version: 0.1.0
type: application
EOF

# Use the starter
helm create myapp --starter=myorg-starter

# The new chart inherits files from the starter template
# Great for enforcing organizational standards!

19.3 Chart Boilerplate Generation

Beyond starters, tools like helmify, chart-builder, and custom scripts auto-generate charts from existing Kubernetes manifests or templates.

Boilerplate Tools
# helmify: Convert existing K8s YAML to Helm chart
kubectl get deploy,svc,cm,secret myapp -o yaml | helmify myapp-chart

# Generate from existing manifests
cat deploy.yaml svc.yaml | helmify generated-chart

19.4 Environment-Specific Patterns

Proven patterns for managing dev/staging/prod differences cleanly — without duplicating charts.

Three Environment Patterns
  PATTERN 1: Multiple Values Files (Simplest — Recommended)
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  chart/
    values.yaml          ← Common defaults
    values-dev.yaml      ← Dev overrides (replicaCount: 1)
    values-staging.yaml  ← Staging overrides (replicaCount: 2)
    values-prod.yaml     ← Prod overrides (replicaCount: 5)
  Deploy: helm install app ./chart -f values-<env>.yaml -n <env>

  PATTERN 2: Environment Key in values.yaml
  ─────────────────────────────────────────
  environment: "dev"    # Switch in values.yaml
  Templates use: {{ if eq .Values.environment "prod" }}...

  PATTERN 3: Separate Charts per Environment
  ──────────────────────────────────────────
  Only when environments are RADICALLY different.
  Not recommended — duplicating chart logic is error-prone.

19.5 Feature Toggles & Conditional Resources

Use boolean values to toggle entire resources or features on/off without changing templates.

Feature Toggle Example
# values.yaml
features:
  ingress: true
  autoscaling: true
  monitoring: false       # Toggle the entire ServiceMonitor
  serviceMesh: false     # Toggle Istio sidecar injection

# templates/servicemonitor.yaml
{{ if .Values.features.monitoring }}
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: ServiceMonitor
# ... full monitor spec ...
{{ end }}

# Install with toggles:
helm install app ./chart --set features.monitoring=true

19.6 Post-Renderers — Kustomize + Helm Integration

Post-renderers let you modify Helm's output before it's applied to Kubernetes. The most common use case: running Kustomize on Helm-rendered manifests.

Post-Renderer Pipeline
  ┌──────────┐     ┌────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────┐
  │  Helm    │────▶│  Rendered  │────▶│  Post-       │────▶│  K8s API │
  │  Template│     │  YAML      │     │  Renderer    │     │  Server  │
  │  Engine  │     │            │     │  (Kustomize) │     │          │
  └──────────┘     └────────────┘     └──────────────┘     └──────────┘
                                          │
                                          │ Applies patches,
                                          │ namespace overrides,
                                          │ common labels, etc.

  USAGE:
  helm install myapp ./chart   --post-renderer ./kustomize-wrapper.sh

  # kustomize-wrapper.sh:
  #!/bin/bash
  cat <&0 > /tmp/helm-output.yaml
  kustomize build --enable-helm | kubectl apply -f -
🔀
When to Use Post-Renderers

When you need Kustomize-style patches on Helm output (common labels, namespace overrides, strategic merges) without modifying the chart. Also: injecting sidecars, adding annotations that the chart doesn't support, enforcing organizational policies.

⚠️
Post-Renderer Caveats

Post-renderers break Helm's "single source of truth" model. Changes made by the renderer are invisible to Helm — helm get manifest won't show them. Use sparingly and document clearly. Prefer modifying values.yaml or templates over post-rendering.

Advanced Patterns Decision Guide — Which Pattern When?
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ADVANCED HELM PATTERNS — WHEN TO USE EACH                                │
  │                                                                           │
  │  Pattern              Use When...                    Exam Relevance        │
  │  ───────────────────  ─────────────────────────────  ──────────────────   │
  │  Library Charts       Multiple charts share the      🟢 High — conceptual │
  │                       same template logic (labels,                        │
  │                       deployment specs)                                   │
  │                                                                           │
  │  Starter Charts       Your org has a standard        🟡 Medium — practical │
  │                       chart scaffold everyone                              │
  │                       should use                                          │
  │                                                                           │
  │  Feature Toggles      One chart needs to work        🟢 High — common     │
  │                       in multiple configurations                          │
  │                       (monitoring on/off, etc.)                           │
  │                                                                           │
  │  Post-Renderers       You MUST patch Helm output     🟡 Medium — edge case │
  │                       without modifying the chart                         │
  │                       (org policies, sidecars)                            │
  │                                                                           │
  │  Environment Files    Different config per env       🟢 High — fundamental │
  │                       (dev/staging/prod)                                  │
  │                                                                           │
  │  🔑 MASTER RULE: Start with environment files. Add feature toggles.      │
  │     Use library charts when you hit copy-paste. Post-renderers last.      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📚Library ChartsShared template code
🚀StartersScaffold templates
⚙️Boilerplatehelmify & tools
🌍Multi-EnvValues file pattern
🎚️TogglesConditional resources
🔀Post-RenderKustomize + Helm

19.7 Post-Renderers - Helm + Kustomize Integration

Post-renderers let you modify rendered YAML AFTER Helm template rendering but BEFORE applying to Kubernetes. This enables combining Helm's templating with Kustomize's patching.

Post-Renderer Pipeline
values.yaml          templates/            kustomization.yaml
    |                     |                       |
    v                     v                       |
+-----------------------------+                   |
| Helm Template Engine        |                   |
| (Go Templates + Sprig)     |                   |
+-------------+---------------+                   |
              |                                   |
              v                                   v
         Rendered YAML    +    Kustomize Patches
              |                     |
              +----------+----------+
                         |
                         v
              +-------------------+
              | Post-Renderer     |
              | (kustomize build) |
              +---------+---------+
                        |
                        v
              Final YAML -> kubectl apply

helm install anihpj ./chart \
  --post-renderer ./kustomize-wrapper.sh

# kustomize-wrapper.sh:
#!/bin/bash
cat <&0 > rendered.yaml
kustomize build . && rm rendered.yaml

# kustomization.yaml:
resources:
- rendered.yaml
patchesStrategicMerge:
- increase-replicas.yaml
EXAM
When to use Post-Renderers: Use them when you need Kustomize-style patching on top of Helm templating. Common use cases: adding common labels to ALL resources, injecting sidecars, or applying organization-specific security policies that shouldn't be in the chart.

19.8 Feature Toggles & Conditional Resources

Use values to control which resources are deployed. This is essential for creating flexible charts that adapt to different environments.

Toggle PatternTemplate CodeUse Case
Resource Toggle{{ if .Values.ingress.enabled }}...{{ end }}Enable/disable entire resources (Ingress, HPA, PVC)
Feature Flag{{ if .Values.features.monitoring }}...{{ end }}Enable features (Prometheus annotations, sidecars)
Environment Switch{{ if eq .Values.env "prod" }}...{{ end }}Environment-specific behavior (production-only resources)
Version Gating{{ if semverCompare ">=1.25" .Capabilities.KubeVersion.GitVersion }}...{{ end }}API version compatibility across clusters
Multi-Tenant{{ if .Values.tenant.isShared }}...{{ end }}Shared vs dedicated tenant resources

19.9 Starter Charts - Organizational Standards

Starter charts are templates for helm create. They encode your organization's standards so every new chart starts compliant.

# Create a starter chart:
mkdir -p $HELM_HOME/starters/microservice/
cp -r my-standard-chart/* $HELM_HOME/starters/microservice/

# Use the starter:
helm create my-svc --starter=microservice

# STARTER CHART BEST PRACTICES:
# 1. Include pre-configured _helpers.tpl with org-standard labels
# 2. Pre-set securityContext with non-root user
# 3. Include resource limits/requests with sensible defaults
# 4. Pre-configure liveness/readiness probes
# 5. Add .helmignore for common patterns (node_modules, .git, *.md)
# 6. Include values.schema.json for validation

19.10 Chart Schema Evolution & Deprecation Strategy

As charts evolve, you need strategies for handling breaking changes in values.yaml without breaking existing deployments.

1
Add, Don't Remove

New values should be ADDED with sensible defaults. Old values should be KEPT but marked as deprecated. Never remove a value key that existing deployments might reference.

# values.yaml v2.0 — BACKWARDS COMPATIBLE:
replicaCount: 3
image:  # OLD way (deprecated, still works)
  repository: anihpj
  tag: v2.0
imageRef: anihpj:v2.0  # NEW way (preferred)
# Template handles both:
image: "{{ .Values.imageRef | default (printf "%s:%s" .Values.image.repository .Values.image.tag) }}"
2
Deprecation Warnings

Use NOTES.txt to warn users about deprecated values. Use required for values being removed in the next major version.

{{ if .Values.image.repository }}
NOTE: 'image.repository' is deprecated. Use 'imageRef' instead.
{{ end }}
3
Major Version Bumps

Bump the chart MAJOR version when removing deprecated values. Users can pin to the old major version until they migrate.

19.11 Multi-Architecture Chart Patterns

Support ARM64, AMD64, and other architectures in a single chart using .Capabilities and template conditionals.

# values.yaml
image:
  repository: anihpj
  tag: v2.0
  
# Auto-detect architecture in templates:
{{ $arch := .Values.arch | default "amd64" }}

# Or detect from node:
nodeSelector:
  kubernetes.io/arch: {{ $arch }}

# Multi-arch image tag pattern:
image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}-{{ $arch }}"
# Produces: anihpj:v2.0-amd64 or anihpj:v2.0-arm64

# For multi-arch manifest images (preferred):
image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
# Single tag, registry serves correct arch automatically
💡
Production Tip: Use multi-arch manifest images (OCI image indexes) whenever possible. A single image tag that works on both ARM and AMD removes the need for architecture-specific templates. Only use arch-specific templates when targeting specialized hardware (GPU, edge devices).
Q1
What is a Library Chart and how is it different from an Application Chart?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

A Library Chart (type: library) contains only named templates — it is NOT deployable. Application Charts (type: application) are deployable. Library charts provide reusable template snippets imported by other charts via dependencies.

Explanation

Think of library charts as "template-only modules." They define {{ define "..." }} blocks that consuming charts invoke with {{ include "..." . }}. This enables DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) for common template patterns like standard labels, deployment specs, or security contexts across multiple charts.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Chart.yaml with dependencies:
dependencies:
  - name: postgresql
    version: "12.x.x"
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
    condition: postgresql.enabled
  - name: redis
    version: "~18.0.0"
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
    tags:
      - cache

# After adding deps, always run:
helm dependency update
# Downloads .tgz to charts/ and creates Chart.lock

# Then install (dependencies auto-included):
helm install myapp ./chart -n prod
Q2
How do you create a chart from a starter template?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

helm create myapp --starter=<starter-name>. Starter charts live in $HELM_HOME/starters/. They're templates for helm create — scaffolding your organization's standard chart structure.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# template vs include - Key Difference:

# template: writes directly to output (NO piping)
{{ template "mylib.labels" . }}

# include: returns a string (CAN pipe through functions)
{{ include "mylib.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
{{ include "mylib.labels" . | quote }}

# Named template definition:
{{- define "anihpj.labels" -}}
app.kubernetes.io/name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }}
{{- end }}

# Usage:
metadata:
  labels:
    {{- include "anihpj.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
Q3
What is a Post-Renderer in Helm?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

A script or binary that modifies Helm's rendered YAML before it's applied to Kubernetes. Used with --post-renderer flag. Common use: running Kustomize on Helm output to add patches, labels, or namespace overrides.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Namespace best practices:

# Create namespace on install:
helm install app ./chart -n myapp --create-namespace

# Deploy same chart to multiple namespaces:
helm install app-dev ./chart -f values-dev.yaml -n dev
helm install app-stg ./chart -f values-stg.yaml -n staging
helm install app-prod ./chart -f values-prod.yaml -n production

# List releases per namespace:
helm list -n dev
helm list -n staging
helm list -n production

# Cross-namespace listing:
helm list -A | grep anihpj
Q4
How do you conditionally enable/disable a resource with feature toggles?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Wrap the resource in an if block: {{ if .Values.features.monitoring }}...resource YAML...{{ end }}. Set features.monitoring: true/false in values.yaml to toggle. One boolean controls the entire resource.

Explanation

Helm uses if for conditionals: {{ if .Values.ingress.enabled }}...{{ end }}. Wrap entire resources. Use eq, ne, lt, gt, and, or, not for comparisons. Resource-level conditionals are standard practice.

Q5
What's the recommended pattern for managing dev/staging/prod environments with Helm?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Multiple values files: One chart with values-dev.yaml, values-staging.yaml, values-prod.yaml. Deploy: helm install app ./chart -f values-<env>.yaml -n <env>. This keeps a single source of truth for templates.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Standard install command:
helm install RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE --create-namespace

# Install with values file:
helm install RELEASE ./chart -f values.yaml -n NAMESPACE

# Install with --set overrides:
helm install RELEASE ./chart --set image.tag=v2.0 -n NAMESPACE

# Install with --atomic (auto-rollback on failure):
helm install RELEASE ./chart -n NAMESPACE --atomic --wait --timeout 5m
Q6
What does helmify do?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Converts existing Kubernetes YAML manifests into a Helm chart. Takes plain YAML files as input and generates Chart.yaml, templates/, and values.yaml with parameterized fields extracted from the manifests.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Minimal valid Chart.yaml:
apiVersion: v2
name: mychart
version: 0.1.0
type: application

# Full Chart.yaml reference:
apiVersion: v2
name: anihpj
version: 0.2.0
appVersion: "2.1.0"
description: A Helm chart for the anihpj job board application
type: application
kubeVersion: ">=1.25.0-0"
maintainers:
  - name: DevOps Team
    email: devops@example.com
icon: https://example.com/anihpj-icon.svg
keywords:
  - django
  - job-board
  - python
Q7
Why would you use a Library Chart instead of duplicating template code?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Library charts enforce DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself). Define shared templates once (labels, deployments, security contexts) and import them across all charts. Fix a bug in the library chart → all consuming charts are updated.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# template vs include - Key Difference:

# template: writes directly to output (NO piping)
{{ template "mylib.labels" . }}

# include: returns a string (CAN pipe through functions)
{{ include "mylib.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
{{ include "mylib.labels" . | quote }}

# Named template definition:
{{- define "anihpj.labels" -}}
app.kubernetes.io/name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }}
{{- end }}

# Usage:
metadata:
  labels:
    {{- include "anihpj.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
Q8
What is a downside of Post-Renderers?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Post-renderer changes are invisible to Helm. helm get manifest shows the pre-rendered output, not what was actually applied. This creates a discrepancy between Helm's stored state and live state — making debugging harder.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

# Inspect a deployed release:

# Get rendered manifests:
helm get manifest RELEASE -n NAMESPACE

# Get user-supplied values:
helm get values RELEASE -n NAMESPACE

# Get ALL computed values (user + defaults):
helm get values RELEASE -n NAMESPACE --all

# Get hooks:
helm get hooks RELEASE -n NAMESPACE

# Get NOTES.txt output:
helm get notes RELEASE -n NAMESPACE

# Current status:
helm status RELEASE -n NAMESPACE

How do you generate boilerplate charts from existing K8s resources?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Use helmify: kubectl get deploy,svc,cm myapp -o yaml | helmify myapp-chart. Or write a custom script that extracts values into values.yaml and replaces them with template expressions. Manual approach: helm create + customize.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.

  pullPolicy: IfNotPresent   # Image pull policy

  port: 80                   # Service port

Q10
What's the difference between Starter Charts and Library Charts?
Answer & Explanation
Answer

Starter Charts: Templates for helm create — used at chart creation time to scaffold new charts. Library Charts: Runtime template dependencies — imported at render time by other charts. Starter = scaffolding tool, Library = shared code module.

Explanation

This concept is frequently tested on the Helm certification exam. The illustration below demonstrates the practical application with real commands and examples you can use directly in the exam terminal.
